Listen
00:00

The Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB), in a letter to Adani Green Energy Ltd, has directed it to stop excavation and construction work linked to its Tarali hydropower project in Satara district.

It said the “excavation/development work” at Sawarghar village was done without permission from the MPCB and without obtaining environmental clearance. The company has said these are construction-support facilities and do not form part of the permanent project components, which “have the requisite statutory clearances”.

This comes amid the controversy over Adani Green’s affidavit regarding the cost of the 1,500 MW Pumped Storage Project (PSP), proposed on the Tarali dam reservoir.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The Indian Express reported that the renewable energy company ow­ned by the Adani Group had sought to sharply revise the declared cost of its 1,500 MW hydropower project to Rs 56.75 crore from Rs 5,675 crore. This revision proportionally reduced the amount the company was required to deposit towards wildlife conservation and protection to Rs 2.27 crore, from Rs 227 crore.

The project spans 150.74 hectares of non-forest land in Nivade, Tondoshi, Kalambe and Jalu villages in Patan taluka of Maharashtra’s Satara district.

Here’s what to know about the project cost revision, the wildlife conservation deposit, and the questions it has raised.

Why was Adani Green Energy asked to deposit Rs 227 crore?

Story continues below this ad

A letter issued by the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEF&CC) on February 11, 2025, recommending the grant of prior Environment Clearance to the Tarali PSP, mentioned the project cost as Rs 5,675 crore.

According to the state forest department, the project falls within the deemed Eco-Sensitive Zone (ESZ) of the Koyna Wildlife Sanctuary in Satara, which is part of the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve (STR). A senior forest officer told The Indian Express that, under existing norms, private companies setting up projects in an ESZ can be asked to deposit up to 4% of the project cost towards conservation and protection.

Also Read | Adani slashes Maharashtra power project cost by 99%, its forest dues plummet; Centre orders probe

Accordingly, at its meeting on February 23, 2026, the State Board for Wildlife (SBWL) laid down 15 conditions for the project. One of these required 4% of the project cost to be deposited in the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve’s bank account.

In a letter to Adani Green Energy dated March 24, 2026, Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (Wildlife) M Shrinivas Reddy listed the 15 conditions laid down by the SBWL and asked the company to deposit Rs 227 crore — 4% of the project cost of Rs 5,675 crore — into the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve Conservation Foundation. Reddy also asked the company to submit an affidavit confirming that it would fulfil the 14 other conditions. The project proposal would then be forwarded to the National Board for Wildlife (NBWL) for consideration.

Story continues below this ad

In another letter to Adani Green Energy, dated May 7, 2026, the Deputy Director of Koyna Wildlife Sanctuary said: “Cost of the project passing through the buffer/deemed eco-sensitive zone of Koyna Wildlife Sanctuary is Rs 5,675 crores and its 4% amounting to Rs 227 crores should be deposited in the bank account of Field Director of STR”.

How did the calculation change to Rs 2.27 crore?

On September 8, 2026, Adani Green Energy’s Chief Operating Officer Naresh Telgu submitted a notarised affidavit regarding the project cost to the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (PCCF), Maharashtra.

The affidavit stated: “While submitting the part IV the cost of the project is considered based on analogous estimation, we considered as INR 56.75 crore, request you to please consider the same as project cost.”

Also Read | Adani project stopped after Rs 227 crore wildlife fee cut to Rs 2.27 crore

On October 12, PCCF Reddy informed Adani Green Energy that his office had accepted the revised project cost of Rs 56.75 crore. He asked the company to immediately deposit 1% of this amount (Rs 56.75 lakh) and pay the remaining 3% (Rs 1.7075 crore) after the NBWL’s approval. The company subsequently deposited Rs 56.75 lakh into the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve’s bank account.

Story continues below this ad

On October 30, Rohan Bhate, Honorary Wildlife Warden of Satara district, registered a complaint on the Prime Minister’s grievance redressal portal and the Maharashtra government’s Aaple Sarkar grievance redressal portal, alleging an “incorrect cost of the project”. On November 6, the MoEF&CC directed the state forest department to investigate the matter on priority. The state forest department has initiated a probe.

What did the company say?

In its first response, an Adani Group spokesperson had said: “All the Tarali PSP elements are within private land ownership across three revenue villages in Patan taluka and have no Forest land. PSPs do not have any adverse impact on the downstream ecology, environment, forest, or wildlife in the area during operations.”

After The Indian Express published its report on November 13, the company issued a statement rejecting the allegation that it had sought to revise the project cost downwards to reduce its statutory obligations.

Also Read | Maharashtra Pollution Control Board stops work at Adani project

The spokesperson said: “The allegation that the company sought to revise project costs downwards to diminish statutory obligations is completely misleading. The online proposal in the Forest/wildlife portal was solely for site investigation purposes, while SBWL considered total project costs of Rs 5,675 crore. Since site investigation costs are around 1% of project costs, therefore clarification of the project Rs 56.75 crore representing solely the site investigations and survey costs, for the online proposal was provided.”

Story continues below this ad

The spokesperson added: “Secondly, the allegation that downward revision was intended to lower conservation costs is false. The Tarali PSP is situated entirely on private, non-forest land and 3.2 kms away from the Koyna wildlife sanctuary. It is outside the notified buffer zone of Sahyadri Tiger reserve and in no way impacts or fringes upon the tiger corridor or any notified Eco Sensitive zone. The project does not cause diversion of any protected areas, any reserve forest or notified Eco Sensitive zone.”

Why did the forest department halt project work?

On November 13, within hours of The Indian Express report, the forest department ordered all work at the Tarali PSP site to stop immediately. The department said work had commenced without prior approval from the NBWL, which it considered mandatory because the project site falls within the deemed ESZ of the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve.

The forest department sought a detailed written explanation from the company, asking it to clarify under what authority and on what basis it had commenced work without NBWL approval. The company was also asked to submit all statutory clearance documents and maps related to the Tarali PSP, along with copies of permissions from the competent authority for cutting trees at the project site.

Responding to the order, Adani Green Energy said in a statement: “No component of the Tarali Pumped Storage Project falls within any notified Protected Area and no forest land is involved in the project. Further, necessary permissions/NOCs relating to land use and statutory requirements have already been obtained from the competent authorities.”

Story continues below this ad

The company also said it had secured Environmental Clearance on February 11, 2025, and Consent to Establish on April 7, 2025, after which construction began. It said wildlife clearance proceedings had been initiated, and that its proposal was pending consideration by the NBWL.

title: From Steve Jobs to Jensen Huang, the unending cult of the American tech founder
content_html:
(From left) Steve Jobs, Sam Altman, Jensen Huang. (Wikimedia Commons, file)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00
AI Translation

Eleven days after he stepped down from Nvidia amid revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Jensen Huang has returned as the chief executive of the artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker.

His reinstatement, following the intervention of US President Donald Trump and mounting pressure from investors, marks one of the most dramatic corporate comebacks in recent Silicon Valley history.

While the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure and subsequent return are unusual, American technology companies have a long history of turning to their founders in times of crisis. From Apple’s Steve Jobs to OpenAI’s Sam Altman, some of the industry’s most prominent executives have returned to lead the companies they helped build, in some instances after being unceremoniously ousted by their boards.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Also Read | What Jensen Huang’s return means for Nvidia and the AI ecosystem

These comebacks also reflect the peculiar relationship that Silicon Valley has with its founders, whose individual personalities, technological vision and ability to command investor confidence can become almost inseparable from the companies they run.

The success of executives such as Jobs has helped perpetuate the belief in Silicon Valley that founders possess an intuitive understanding of their businesses that professional managers cannot easily replicate. However, Huang’s comeback presents a somewhat different proposition. Unlike Jobs, who returned to an Apple facing business challenges, Huang’s reinstatement followed a crisis precipitated by revelations about his own conduct.

His return, even as investigations remain underway, also raises questions about the extent to which the commercial indispensability of a founder can supersede conventional considerations of corporate governance and accountability. There are many unanswered questions around national security, governance and political intervention surrounding Huang’s reinstatement too.

Story continues below this ad

Here is a look at some of Silicon Valley’s most high-profile founder comebacks, the circumstances that led to their return, and how they shaped the fortunes of their companies.

Steve Jobs, Apple (1997)

Arguably the most famous corporate comeback in Silicon Valley’s history is that of Steve Jobs, who co-founded Apple in 1976 with Steve Wozniak.

In 1985, following a bitter power struggle with then Apple CEO John Sculley, whom Jobs himself had recruited from PepsiCo, the company’s board sided with Sculley, leading to Jobs’ departure. He went on to establish computer company NeXT and subsequently acquired the business that became animation studio Pixar.

Steve Jobs with the Macintosh computer in January 1984. He would be fired the next year. (Wikimedia Commons)

By the mid-1990s, Apple was struggling financially and losing ground to Microsoft-powered personal computers. Its acquisition of NeXT brought Jobs back into the company, and in September 1997, he became its interim CEO.

Story continues below this ad

What followed was one of the most remarkable turnarounds in corporate history. Under Jobs, Apple launched the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad — products that fundamentally altered the consumer technology industry. By the time Jobs stepped down in August 2011, Apple had become one of the world’s most valuable companies, and continues to.

Sam Altman, OpenAI (2023)

Perhaps the closest parallel to Huang’s dramatic reinstatement is the return of Sam Altman as OpenAI’s CEO in November 2023 – sans the numerous extramarital affairs.

OpenAI’s board abruptly fired Altman in November 2023, saying that he had not been consistently forthcoming in his communications with directors. The decision came barely a year after the launch of ChatGPT, which had catapulted OpenAI to the forefront of the global AI industry.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. (Wikimedia Commons)

The sacking triggered a revolt within the company, with an overwhelming majority of its employees threatening to leave unless Altman was reinstated. Microsoft, OpenAI’s biggest financial backer at the time, offered to hire Altman and his colleagues.

Story continues below this ad

Also Read | Why is Sarvam AI offering Chinese AI models, and what does it mean for India’s AI ambitions?

Within days, an agreement was reached for Altman’s return, accompanied by an overhaul of OpenAI’s board. An independent review subsequently concluded that his conduct did not warrant his removal.

The episode demonstrated how even a board specifically constituted to prioritise the safe development of AI could find itself at odds with the commercial interests of investors and employees.

Michael Dell, Dell (2007)

Michael Dell, who founded his eponymous computer company in 1984, while retaining the position of chairman. His successor, Kevin Rollins, struggled with intensifying competition and slowing growth, prompting Dell’s return as CEO in January 2007.

Story continues below this ad
Michael Dell stepped down as Dell CEO in 2004 but returned in 2007. (Wikimedia Commons)

In 2013, Dell took the company private in a $24.9-billion deal with private equity firm Silver Lake, allowing it to undertake a restructuring away from the scrutiny of public markets.

Three years later, the company acquired data storage giant EMC in a landmark technology deal, transforming Dell from a business largely associated with personal computers into a major enterprise technology and computing infrastructure company.

Jack Dorsey, Twitter (2015)

Jack Dorsey, Twitter’s co-founder and first CEO, was pushed out of the position in 2008 amid concerns over his management of the fledgling social media platform.

Jack Dorsey returned as Twitter CEO in 2015. (Wikimedia Commons)

In 2015, as Twitter struggled to expand its user base and faced pressure from investors, Dorsey returned as CEO following Dick Costolo’s resignation. For the next six years, he simultaneously ran Twitter and payments company Square.

Story continues below this ad

When Dorsey stepped down again in November 2021, handing over the reins to India-born Parag Agrawal, he explicitly questioned the culture of founder-led technology companies, arguing that excessive dependence on founders could become a limitation for businesses.

Larry Page, Google (2011)

Google co-founder Larry Page relinquished the CEO position in 2001 to Eric Schmidt, an experienced technology executive brought in to manage the rapidly expanding company.

In 2015, Larry Page oversaw Google’s corporate restructuring under a new parent company, Alphabet. (Wikimedia Commons)

A decade later, Page reclaimed the position, with Schmidt becoming executive chairman. Unlike several other high-profile founder comebacks, the transition was not precipitated by an acrimonious boardroom battle.

In 2015, Page oversaw Google’s corporate restructuring under a new parent company, Alphabet, allowing its core Internet business and more experimental technological ventures to operate separately. He became Alphabet’s CEO, while Sundar Pichai took charge of Google.

By the mid-1990s, Apple was struggling financially and losing ground to Microsoft-powered personal computers. Its acquisition of NeXT brought Jobs back into the company, and in September 1997, he became its interim CEO.
Story continues below this ad
What followed was one of the most remarkable turnarounds in corporate history. Under Jobs, Apple launched the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad — products that fundamentally altered the consumer technology industry. By the time Jobs stepped down in August 2011, Apple had become one of the world’s most valuable companies, and continues to.
Sam Altman, OpenAI (2023)
Perhaps the closest parallel to Huang’s dramatic reinstatement is the return of Sam Altman as OpenAI’s CEO in November 2023 – sans the numerous extramarital affairs.
OpenAI’s board abruptly fired Altman in November 2023, saying that he had not been consistently forthcoming in his communications with directors. The decision came barely a year after the launch of ChatGPT, which had catapulted OpenAI to the forefront of the global AI industry.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. (Wikimedia Commons)
The sacking triggered a revolt within the company, with an overwhelming majority of its employees threatening to leave unless Altman was reinstated. Microsoft, OpenAI’s biggest financial backer at the time, offered to hire Altman and his colleagues.

Within days, an agreement was reached for Altman’s return, accompanied by an overhaul of OpenAI’s board. An independent review subsequently concluded that his conduct did not warrant his removal.
The episode demonstrated how even a board specifically constituted to prioritise the safe development of AI could find itself at odds with the commercial interests of investors and employees.
Michael Dell, Dell (2007)
Michael Dell, who founded his eponymous computer company in 1984, while retaining the position of chairman. His successor, Kevin Rollins, struggled with intensifying competition and slowing growth, prompting Dell’s return as CEO in January 2007.
Story continues below this ad
Michael Dell stepped down as Dell CEO in 2004 but returned in 2007. (Wikimedia Commons)
In 2013, Dell took the company private in a $24.9-billion deal with private equity firm Silver Lake, allowing it to undertake a restructuring away from the scrutiny of public markets.
Three years later, the company acquired data storage giant EMC in a landmark technology deal, transforming Dell from a business largely associated with personal computers into a major enterprise technology and computing infrastructure company.
Jack Dorsey, Twitter (2015)
Jack Dorsey, Twitter’s co-founder and first CEO, was pushed out of the position in 2008 amid concerns over his management of the fledgling social media platform.
Jack Dorsey returned as Twitter CEO in 2015. (Wikimedia Commons)
In 2015, as Twitter struggled to expand its user base and faced pressure from investors, Dorsey returned as CEO following Dick Costolo’s resignation. For the next six years, he simultaneously ran Twitter and payments company Square.
Story continues below this ad
When Dorsey stepped down again in November 2021, handing over the reins to India-born Parag Agrawal, he explicitly questioned the culture of founder-led technology companies, arguing that excessive dependence on founders could become a limitation for businesses.
Larry Page, Google (2011)
Google co-founder Larry Page relinquished the CEO position in 2001 to Eric Schmidt, an experienced technology executive brought in to manage the rapidly expanding company.
In 2015, Larry Page oversaw Google’s corporate restructuring under a new parent company, Alphabet. (Wikimedia Commons)
A decade later, Page reclaimed the position, with Schmidt becoming executive chairman. Unlike several other high-profile founder comebacks, the transition was not precipitated by an acrimonious boardroom battle.
In 2015, Page oversaw Google’s corporate restructuring under a new parent company, Alphabet, allowing its core Internet business and more experimental technological ventures to operate separately. He became Alphabet’s CEO, while Sundar Pichai took charge of Google.

title: AI stocks rebound: How Nvidia’s comeback lifted Asian and US markets
content_html:
A dealer walks near the screens showing the Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) and the foreign exchange rate between U.S. dollar and South Korean won at a dealing room of Hana Bank, Friday, November 20. (AP)

Listen

AI Translation

Asian and American stock markets were in a lull in November amid anxiety that the AI (artificial intelligence) bubble could pop. That was until Jensen Huang’s comeback into the top job at Nvidia, which lifted these AI-driven markets to their best day in months.

After a sharp crash following Huang’s resignation earlier in the month, the US’ clean chit on the Chinese spy controversy and his comeback to Nvidia led to the chipmaker regaining nearly a third of its value, lifting other AI-led markets in the process.

Lull period for AI-led markets

The US markets have had a poor month so far, dropping as much as 11% until the sharp gains on Monday. The AI-related fears have pulled down the share prices of big names like Google’s parent company Alphabet, the newly-listed Anthropic, and Meta, among others.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

These AI fears deepened after Huang, a top name in the AI space, exited the company, and after Democrats’ thumping win in the mid-term elections sparked concerns about a slowdown in AI spending.

Also Read | In Jensen Huang’s return, unanswered questions of national security, governance and politics

The rut had been far deeper for Asian markets that are largely driven by AI. After reaching record highs amid AI optimism earlier this year, the South Korean, Japanese, and Taiwanese markets had fallen sharply from their peaks till Monday. The South Korean Kospi index had lost nearly half its value. The Japanese and Taiwanese indices had lost 20-30%.

While the US had some of the biggest names in the AI and tech space, Asian markets like Taiwan and South Korea are largely driven by AI stocks. For example, chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix hold almost half the weightage on the Kospi, while TSMC alone accounts for 40% of Taiwan’s benchmark index.

Huang’s return lifts sentiment

Nvidia’s board announced Huang’s return late on Monday, days after ruling out any such possibilities. US President Donald Trump also expressed support for this decision, giving Huang a clean chit on his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Story continues below this ad

His reinstatement lifted shares of Nvidia, which had crashed over 40% since his extramarital affair allegations first surfaced in late October, by 31.5% – the biggest single-day gain since 2003. Other AI players like Meta, Alphabet, and Oracle shot up by 6-12%. This lifted the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite index by 6.5%, helping Wall Street recover from the 8% selloff last week.

Also Read | From Steve Jobs to Jensen Huang, the unending cult of the American tech founder

“Nvidia is the biggest and most important name in AI, and the whole industry is dependent on their chips. And Nvidia and Huang are synonymous. So his comeback is a big positive for the industry in terms of stability and direction,” a head of research at a domestic broking firm said.

Major firms like Morgan Stanley and Bernstein, which had downgraded their view on Nvidia after Huang’s exit, calling it a “big setback”, also started to reverse their opinion after his comeback. Bernstein, for example, upgraded their rating on the stock on Monday, just days after downgrading it post Huang’s resignation.

The comeback also sparked a rally across Asia. The Kospi jumped 7% early on Tuesday. Taiwan’s Taiex index skyrocketed 9%. Japan’s Nikkei 225 also gained 4%. While the Indian markets are shut on the occasion of Prakash Gurpurb Sri Guru Nanak Dev, the GIFT Nifty was up 0.4%, signalling that the benchmark Nifty 50 and Sensex may open on a positive note on Wednesday.

title: In Jensen Huang’s return, unanswered questions of national security, governance and politics
content_html:
President Donald Trump looks on as Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, speaks during an event at the White House in Washington, April 30, 2025. (NYT)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Less than two weeks after he stepped down as the chief executive of Nvidia amid revelations of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Jensen Huang is back at the helm of the world’s most consequential artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker. His dramatic reinstatement on Monday (November 23) has triggered a euphoric response on Wall Street, but a bipartisan backlash in Washington.

While Huang’s return has brought an end to an unprecedented leadership crisis at Nvidia, several of the questions that precipitated his departure remain unanswered – from the extent of the potential national security risks posed by his relationship to the standards of corporate governance at the chipmaker, and the propriety of the White House’s intervention even as multiple investigations remain underway.

At the heart of the controversy is also a larger tension, as to whether the enormous economic and strategic significance of Nvidia, whose chips underpin much of the global AI industry, has complicated the ability of American institutions to hold its leadership accountable.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Nvidia’s shares rose 31.5% on Monday, adding roughly $950 billion to its market capitalisation. But even as investors celebrated Huang’s return, lawmakers from both the Republican and Democratic parties questioned the circumstances under which the company’s board reversed its earlier decision.

The national security question remains unresolved

Huang’s troubles stemmed from his relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman formerly associated with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has been under scrutiny over the suspected diversion of advanced Nvidia chips to China. US intelligence officials reportedly suspect her of having worked for Chinese intelligence, an allegation Beijing has denied.

The concerns are particularly significant given Washington’s attempts to restrict Beijing’s access to advanced American semiconductors, which can be used for developing sophisticated AI systems and have potential military applications.

Also in Explained | Why Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO

In announcing Huang’s reinstatement, Nvidia’s board said it had received inputs from senior officials in the US government and was confident that his return posed no national security risk. However, it neither identified these officials nor disclosed the nature of the information they had provided.

Story continues below this ad

Crucially, Nvidia said its own investigation, being conducted by a committee of independent directors with the assistance of external legal counsel, would continue. Huang has committed to cooperating with the investigation.

Separately, on the same day that Huang returned, the Trump administration moved to add Megaspeed and several associated entities to its trade blacklist, restricting their access to sensitive American technology.

In a joint statement last week, the US Departments of Justice and Commerce said Nvidia had stopped selling chips to Megaspeed in June 2025. Investigations into the suspected diversion of chips remain underway. No evidence establishing Huang’s personal involvement in espionage or illegal chip shipments has been made public.

The board’s U-turn raises questions of corporate governance

As recently as November 17, Nvidia’s board chairman Harvey Jones had categorically ruled out Huang’s return as CEO, telling investors during the company’s earnings call that the executive’s personal conduct was inconsistent with the chipmaker’s standards and values.

Story continues below this ad

Six days later, the board unanimously voted to reinstate him, saying that following several meetings with Huang, it was satisfied with his forthrightness and ability to lead the company. However, it offered little explanation about how the concerns over his personal conduct had been addressed.

Apart from his relationship with Alice Huang, the Nvidia co-founder reportedly had affairs with two employees of the chipmaker, including Kimberly Powell, its vice president of healthcare, according to Reuters. Huang has publicly acknowledged marital infidelity but has not individually addressed all the reported relationships. He has since also admitted to having affairs with more women than previously reported.

Also Read | What Jensen Huang’s return means for Nvidia and the AI ecosystem

These revelations raise questions separate from those concerning national security, including about workplace power dynamics, potential conflicts of interest and the board’s oversight of its chief executive. They also give a rare insight into how Nvidia operated, and how the cult of power surrounding Huang – paired with the chipmaker’s astronomical rise in fortunes – have effectively made him and the company too big to fail.

Trump’s intervention and questions of conflict of interest

In an extraordinary instance of a sitting US President intervening in the leadership affairs of a publicly listed company, Donald Trump acknowledged on Monday that he had personally persuaded Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back.

Story continues below this ad

“And I convinced them. I made the deal,” Trump told CNBC.

Trump also claimed that US Attorney General Todd Blanche had confirmed that the government did not possess evidence of unlawful conduct by Huang. However, the absence of evidence of criminal wrongdoing does not necessarily address the broader concerns about potential national security vulnerabilities.

There is also a financial dimension to Trump’s intervention. According to a Reuters analysis of his financial disclosures, the President owns Nvidia shares worth between $11 million and $55 million. Monday’s rally could have increased his net worth by as much as $17 million.

The White House has maintained that Trump’s investments were independently managed and that neither the President nor his family could influence investment decisions. Trump’s intervention is particularly also consequential given Huang’s sustained lobbying of the US administration to ease restrictions on the sale of AI chips to China, an important market for Nvidia.

A bipartisan backlash, and more investigations

Story continues below this ad

Huang’s reinstatement has drawn criticism even from within Trump’s Republican Party.

Republican Senator John Curtis questioned which government officials had advised Nvidia’s board, what information they had provided, and how the company had arrived at its assessment while its independent investigation remained incomplete.

“Nvidia’s board says it relied on input from senior US officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk. I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” Curtis wrote in a social media post on X. “Last week, the board said it didn’t intend to reinstate him. I’d like to know what changed.”

Also Read | What Democrat-controlled US Congress means for AI, trade, immigration, oil

Republican Senators Pete Ricketts and Kevin Cramer also criticised the decision, with the latter arguing that while Nvidia’s board would bear the legal and reputational risks of bringing Huang back, any national security consequences would extend to American citizens and the military.

Story continues below this ad

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren called the decision reckless and demanded that the Trump administration explain its role to Congress. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer promised investigations into any wrongdoing by the administration and Nvidia executives.

Separately, California Attorney General Rob Bonta has issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia to ascertain whether the company or Huang’s actions enabled China to obtain advanced chips or confidential information, and whether the chipmaker misled investors about such risks.

The controversy is unlikely to die down anytime soon, particularly with Democrats set to take control of Congress in January. Huang is scheduled to appear before lawmakers for closed-door questioning on December 1, followed by a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3.

title: Ganga Water Treaty: Will the 1996 pact be renewed? Where India, Bangladesh stand
content_html:
The Farakka barrage. Photo: Partha Paul
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Less than three weeks before the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty officially lapses on December 12, representatives from India and Bangladesh met in Dhaka this weekend (November 21-22) for the 91st routine meeting of the India-Bangladesh Joint Committee.

Although there was no official word on whether discussions for renewing the 1996 bilateral treaty were held, some reports have indicated that Bangladesh appears to be agreeable to the prospect of renewing the pact instead of seeking a fresh agreement altogether.

How did the treaty come to be, what are its provisions, and where do both countries currently stand on renegotiating the terms of engagement? We explain.

From friction to friendship

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Tensions had brewed over sharing of the Ganga waters since the 1950s, when the Indian government proposed building a barrage at Farakka in West Bengal, some 18 km from what would become the international border between India and (then) East Pakistan. Construction began in 1961, and upon its completion in 1975, the Farakka barrage started diverting waters from the Ganga to the Hooghly river, flushing out the silt around the Kolkata port located on the latter and keeping it navigable for ships.

But throughout its construction, friction remained and reached a flashpoint in 1976 when Maulana Bhashani, an Awami League party legislator in (by then independent) Bangladesh, led the “Farakka Long March” against India’s water policies, demanding the demolition of the barrage, which he argued had resulted in the drying up of the Padma river (Ganga’s main distributary in Bangladesh) and subsequent desertification.

Also read | The next India-Bangladesh Ganges treaty must also protect the river

Although there were ad hoc agreements signed between the two countries throughout the next decade (1977, 1982, and 1985), none of them provided lasting solutions.

Finally, in December 1996, both countries under the leadership of Prime Ministers H D Deve Gowda and Sheikh Hasina signed the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty, instituting a 30-year framework for a flow-sharing mechanism during the annual dry season (January to May) and setting up a joint committee to monitor and implement the pact.

Story continues below this ad

Ganga Water Sharing Treaty: Terms of agreement

The treaty, hailed as a milestone in bilateral diplomacy at the time, established a three-tiered allocation system based on historical data of average flow during a 10-day period between 1949 and 1988.

Under the agreement, if the flow of water falls to or below the lower threshold of 70,000 cusecs (cubic feet per second, the unit to measure flow), the two countries would share the water equally. If the flow is between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, then Bangladesh would be entitled to 35,000 cusecs and India was to keep the remaining flow. In the event of the upper threshold of 75,000 cusecs or more, India would get 40,000 and Bangladesh would receive the balance (see table).

Annexure I of the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty.

The aforementioned terms were subject to an additional clause: between March 11 and May 10 each year, both countries would receive a guaranteed 35,000 cusecs of water in alternate three 10-day periods.

Although it lacks a minimum guarantee clause, the treaty has an emergency provision: Article II(iii) states that “in the event flow at Farakka falls below 50,000 cusecs in any 10-day period, the two Governments will enter into immediate consultations to make adjustments on an emergency basis, in accordance with the principles of equity, fair play and no harm to either party”.

Story continues below this ad

For resolving disputes, the Joint Committee (consisting of an equal number of representatives nominated by both governments) would be primarily responsible, failing which it would be referred to the Joint Rivers Commission (JRC). The two countries had set up the JRC in 1972 as a bilateral mechanism to deliberate and manage water sharing for 54 shared rivers, of which only the Ganga is governed by a formal treaty as of today.

Sticking points

Over the years, the treaty has been criticised in both countries for not accounting for the future needs of rising populations in both countries, besides climate change-induced crises. Although the treaty provides for renewal by mutual consent at the end of the 30-year period, both sides have indicated a willingness to revisit the agreement’s terms.

News reports from last year suggested India was seeking an additional 30,000 to 35,000 cusecs during the March 11-May 10 period to meet its growing needs, and that the new treaty could be relatively shorter in duration, that is, 10 to 15 years. PTI reported that during a JRC meeting, Bangladesh had asked for a guaranteed release of 40,000 cusecs of water between February and May, besides a longer treaty renewal period and enhanced flood data sharing.

One point of contention has been Bangladesh’s demand to reinstate a minimum guarantee, similar to what was laid down in the 1977 ad hoc agreement. This provision guaranteed that Bangladesh received at least 80% of its scheduled allocation during certain lean-season periods, even when actual availability fell short.

Story continues below this ad

Nilanjan Ghosh, who heads Development Studies at the think tank Observer Research Foundation (ORF), wrote in a piece for the ORF website: “A fixed volumetric guarantee that remains binding irrespective of actual flows could impose an asymmetric burden of hydrological risk on the upstream country. India therefore cannot commit to such an impracticable demand. This could leave India bearing a disproportionate share of climate-induced shortages, regardless of its domestic needs.”

Also read | Why Bihar wants the Farakka treaty scrapped — and why it puts Centre in a bind

After the Tarique Rahman-led Bangladesh Nationalist Party’s landslide victory in the country’s general election in February 2026, reports had emerged that the treaty’s renewal would be among the top priorities of the newly elected government. But no discussions have been forthcoming on that front, even as tensions continue to simmer between the two countries over the contentious issue of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s extradition, who has been living in exile in New Delhi since her ouster in August 2024. It was understood to be why Tarique Rahman didn’t go ahead with a proposed official visit in August 2026 — it would’ve been his first since becoming prime minister.

The same month, the treaty’s provisions saw resistance brewing in Bihar, where the Janata Dal (United) — an ally of the BJP — pushed against its renewal, saying that the pact had proved “detrimental to Bihar’s interest”.

India’s decision last year to unilaterally put the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan in abeyance after the Pahalgam terror attack in April 2025 has also prompted caution in Bangladesh.

What next

Story continues below this ad

Less than three weeks before the

officially lapses on December 12, representatives from India and Bangladesh met in Dhaka this weekend (November 21-22) for the 91st routine meeting of the India-Bangladesh Joint Committee.
Although there was no official word on whether discussions for renewing the 1996 bilateral treaty were held, some reports have indicated that Bangladesh appears to be agreeable to the prospect of renewing the pact instead of seeking a fresh agreement altogether.
How did the treaty come to be, what are its provisions, and where do both countries currently stand on renegotiating the terms of engagement? We explain.
From friction to friendship
Story continues below.
Subscribe to see fewer ads.
Tensions had brewed over sharing of the Ganga waters since the 1950s, when the Indian government proposed building a barrage at Farakka in West Bengal, some 18 km from what would become the international border between India and (then) East Pakistan. Construction began in 1961, and upon its completion in 1975, the Farakka barrage started diverting waters from the Ganga to the Hooghly river, flushing out the silt around the
Kolkata
port located on the latter and keeping it navigable for ships.
But throughout its construction, friction remained and reached a flashpoint in 1976 when Maulana Bhashani, an Awami League party legislator in (by then independent) Bangladesh, led the “Farakka Long March” against India’s water policies, demanding the demolition of the barrage, which he argued had resulted in the drying up of the Padma river (Ganga’s main distributary in Bangladesh) and subsequent desertification.

Although there were ad hoc agreements signed between the two countries throughout the next decade (1977, 1982, and 1985), none of them provided lasting solutions.
Finally, in December 1996, both countries under the leadership of Prime Ministers H D Deve Gowda and
Sheikh Hasina
signed the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty, instituting a 30-year framework for a flow-sharing mechanism during the annual dry season (January to May) and setting up a joint committee to monitor and implement the pact.
Story continues below this ad
Ganga Water Sharing Treaty: Terms of agreement
The treaty, hailed as a milestone in bilateral diplomacy at the time, established a three-tiered allocation system based on historical data of average flow during a 10-day period between 1949 and 1988.
Under the agreement, if the flow of water falls to or below the lower threshold of 70,000 cusecs (cubic feet per second, the unit to measure flow), the two countries would share the water equally. If the flow is between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, then Bangladesh would be entitled to 35,000 cusecs and India was to keep the remaining flow. In the event of the upper threshold of 75,000 cusecs or more, India would get 40,000 and Bangladesh would receive the balance (
see table

Annexure I of the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty.
The aforementioned terms were subject to an additional clause: between March 11 and May 10 each year, both countries would receive a guaranteed 35,000 cusecs of water in alternate three 10-day periods.
Although it lacks a minimum guarantee clause, the treaty has an emergency provision: Article II(iii) states that “in the event flow at Farakka falls below 50,000 cusecs in any 10-day period, the two Governments will enter into immediate consultations to make adjustments on an emergency basis, in accordance with the principles of equity, fair play and no harm to either party”.

For resolving disputes, the Joint Committee (consisting of an equal number of representatives nominated by both governments) would be primarily responsible, failing which it would be referred to the Joint Rivers Commission (JRC). The two countries had set up the JRC in 1972 as a bilateral mechanism to deliberate and manage water sharing for 54 shared rivers, of which only the Ganga is governed by a formal treaty as of today.
Sticking points
Over the years, the treaty has been criticised in both countries for not accounting for the future needs of rising populations in both countries, besides climate change-induced crises. Although the treaty provides for renewal by mutual consent at the end of the 30-year period, both sides have indicated a willingness to revisit the agreement’s terms.
News reports from last year suggested India was seeking an additional 30,000 to 35,000 cusecs during the March 11-May 10 period to meet its growing needs, and that the new treaty could be relatively shorter in duration, that is, 10 to 15 years.

One point of contention has been Bangladesh’s demand to reinstate a minimum guarantee, similar to what was laid down in the 1977 ad hoc agreement. title: What the Ayodhya-Janakpur train says about India’s railway diplomacy
content_html:
The decorated Saryu-Kamala Express inaugural special train at the Ayodhya Junction on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. (Photo: PTI)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

The Prime Ministers of India and Nepal, Narendra Modi and Balendra Shah, Monday flagged off the first passenger train between the two countries from Ayodhya to Janakpur. Named Sarayu-Kamala Express, the train will cover a distance of over 600 km in around 19 hours and will have stops at Gorakhpur, Basti, Raxaul, Sitamarhi, Madhubani, and Jaynagar.

The move will not only strengthen cross-border connectivity and diplomacy between the two countries, but it also provides a link between two significant religious sites for Hindus — Ayodhya (for Ram) and Janakpur (for Sita).

The project is also part of India Railways’ ambitious Ramayana, Buddhist and Shiv-Shakti circuits by linking Janakpur-Ayodhya, Lumbini-Bodhgaya-Sarnath-Kushinagar and Kathmandu (Pashupatinath)-Varanasi.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

“In 2025 alone, around 30 crore pilgrims from across the country and the world visited Ayodhya. With the launch of the Saryu-Kamala Express train service today, we are adding a new dimension to this sacred bond. This will now make it easier for pilgrims visiting Ayodhya to travel to Janakpur to seek blessings of Mata Sita,” said PM Modi in his address.

He further said that India will work together to enhance connectivity between sacred sites in both countries.

Key projects

India and Nepal share religious, cultural and historical ties. The movement of people between the two countries has remained uninterrupted over the years, with people from either side frequently crossing the border for jobs, tourism, marriages, etc. The Railways have now undertaken several projects traversing these regions to facilitate the seamless cross-border movement of people.

Jaynagar-Bijalpura-Bardibas and Jogbani-Biratnagar are two important ongoing railway projects between India and Nepal. Apart from this, the Raxaul-Kathmandu railway line is another ambitious cross-border project.

Story continues below this ad

Along with the flagging of the express train, the two leaders announced the finalisation of the Field Location Survey for the proposed Raxaul-Kathmandu electrified broad-gauge railway line, and announced that the two sides will collaborate in the development of the East-West Railway in Nepal.

“Apart from these projects, as part of capacity building, Nepal Railway officers and staff have been imparted training on various aspects related to train operations at Gatishakti Vishwavidyalaya, Vadodara,” said a senior Railway official.

Other cross-border projects

Nepal is not the only neighbouring country where Indian Railways is looking to extend its network. Last year in September, the government announced two cross-border railway projects to connect Bhutan with the bordering areas of Assam and West Bengal. The 69-km Kokrajhar (Assam)-Gelephu (Bhutan) and 20-km Banarhat (West Bengal)-Samtse (Bhutan) lines will cost Rs 3,456 crore and Rs 577 crore, respectively.

Currently, the Himalayan nation Bhutan does not have a railway network. It was the result of almost two decades of efforts made by India and Bhutan to formally announce the two strategic projects.

Story continues below this ad

Earlier, India operated cross-border trains Maitree Express and Bandhan Express to Bangladesh, which was suspended in July 2024 following the unrest in the neighbouring country. Bandhan Express used to run between Kolkata (India) and Khulna (Bangaldesh) and Maitree Express between Kolkata to Dhaka Cantonment.

Indian Railways earlier also operated the famous Samjhauta Express and Thar Express between India and Pakistan. Both trains were suspended in August 2019 due to sustained tension between both countries after the government revoked the special status of Jammu & Kashmir.

India has also planned a rail link to Myanmar. The Jiribam-Imphal section (125 Km), which falls within Indian territory, is under construction. The remaining portion from Imphal to Moreh in India is yet to take off and the section from Tamu to Kalay (128) in Myanmar has not been sanctioned.

title: What Jensen Huang’s return means for Nvidia and the AI ecosystem
content_html:
Jensen Huang, co-founder of Nvidia, has officially been reinstated as CEO and President by the Board of Directors (Wikimedia Commons)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Weeks after he had resigned as the chief executive of Nvidia after being embroiled in allegations of extramarital affairs with multiple women including a purported Chinese spy, the chipmaker reinstated Jensen Huang as the CEO of the company late on Monday, after its board found that he posed “no national security risk”.

“Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board,” Nvidia said in a statement, adding that the board’s decision was unanimous. “In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the company said.

US President Donald Trump, who had earlier called for Huang’s return to the chipmaker said the company had made the “correct and proper” decision in reinstating him. “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct (sic),” he said in a social media post.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Nvidia’s stocks, which had faced a selloff trend since Hunag left, surged more than 31% in pre-market trading following the news.

What led to Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s chief

In light of recent reporting that Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the company’s board had formed a committee composed solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C Jones, Chair of Nvidia’s Board.

Upon his reinstatement, said Huang: “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”

Story continues below this ad
Also Read | Behind Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair lies a much bigger China controversy

In light of the allegations, Nvidia’s board had also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee composed solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters.

The company said it was commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across Nvidia.

How the Huang controversy threatened to burst the AI boom

Even before his resignation, the scandal and his expected ouster had sent shockwaves through global financial markets, wiping hundreds of billions of dollars off the chipmaker’s valuation and prompting investors to turn towards rivals such as AMD and Broadcom.

But for many, the implications of the crisis could have extended well beyond the fortunes of Nvidia, given the company’s central position in the AI industry, in which it has emerged as the biggest supplier of computing infrastructure and an important financier of the technology’s expansion.

Story continues below this ad

Jensen Huang’s ouster earlier this month, and the resulting uncertainty for Nvidia, had come at a particularly delicate moment for the industry. Technology firms are committing hundreds of billions of dollars to building data centres and developing increasingly powerful AI models, which run on Nvidia’s highly advanced chips. Much of this investment is flowing into the chipmaker. Any prolonged disruption at the company could, therefore, have consequences for the pace at which the industry expands.

Also Read | Jensen Huang-Alice Huang affair: How the Nvidia scandal became a US security concern

Nvidia’s shares had tanked, and continued the trend, following allegations that Huang engaged in extramarital affairs with at least three women, including Alice Huang, who was said to be a Chinese spy and helped procure banned Nvidia GPUs for Beijing to bypass export control restrictions imposed by Washington.

The reaction reflects how AI has become one of the most consequential investment themes in global equity markets. Nvidia alone accounts for roughly 6% of the S&P 500, making movements in its share price significant for the broader index. The concentration means that even investors without direct exposure to Nvidia can be affected by its fortunes through index funds and other investments.

For many, the bigger concern was not what happened to Nvidia’s immediate chip sales, but whether its crisis could affect the financing arrangements driving the AI infrastructure boom. Nvidia has increasingly evolved from a supplier of computing hardware into an investor and financial backer of the companies building infrastructure around its products.

Story continues below this ad

The key concern stemmed from the fact that should Huang’s long-term successor decide to scale back investments, reconsider financial guarantees or adopt a more conservative approach towards supporting customers, it could have widespread reverberations across the AI ecosystem.

For instance, the company has disclosed approximately $164.5 billion in financial commitments, including an obligation capped at $105 billion relating to an OpenAI data centre in Ohio, alongside more than $50 billion in lease and capacity guarantees.

Such investments have helped accelerate the expansion of data centre capacity. However, they have also raised questions about the extent to which spending across the industry is being supported by financial commitments between companies that are simultaneously suppliers, customers and investors — creating a circular economy.

title: Ayodhya to Janakpur: Faith, strategy behind India-Nepal’s new rail link
content_html:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart, Balendra Shah, jointly flag off the Saryu-Kamala Express at Hyderabad House in New Delhi on Monday. (ANI Photo)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

During his maiden official visit to India, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah and PM Narendra Modi flagged off a train service between Ayodhya and Janakpur. The new Ayodhya-Janakpur Saryu Kamala Express is the first direct passenger train service connecting the two cities in India and Nepal.

While Ayodhya is revered as the birthplace of Lord Ram, Janakpur, in Nepal, is widely believed to be the region ruled by Goddess Sita’s father, King Janaka.

What is the route of the new train? What is the significance of Janakpur in the Ramayana? What is the strategic dimension to these cultural initiatives? We explain.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What is the route of the Ayodhya-Janakpur Saryu Kamala Express?

The weekly train service will cover approximately 604 km between Ayodhya Cantt in Uttar Pradesh and Janakpur Dham in Nepal, passing through several towns in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

The train’s commercial stoppages include Mankapur, Basti and Gorakhpur in Uttar Pradesh; Narkatiaganj, Raxaul, Sitamarhi, Shisho, Madhubani and Jaynagar in Bihar; and Janakpur Dham in Nepal. The journey takes around 19 hours.

The decorated Saryu-Kamala Express inaugural special train, running between Ayodhya in India and Janakpur in Nepal, at the Ayodhya Junction ahead of its flag-off, on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. (PTI Photo)

The service will operate once a week, with its originating days being Saturday from Janakpur and Monday from Ayodhya.

The route is expected to benefit pilgrims travelling between the two religious destinations, as well as passengers travelling for business, education and family-related purposes.

Story continues below this ad

Why is Janakpur significant?

Janakpur, located in Nepal’s Madhesh province in the Terai plains, is an important pilgrimage centre for Hindus. It is associated with the ancient kingdom of Mithila, whose king, Janaka, was Sita’s father. Sita is also known as Janaki, after her father.

The city is home to the Janaki Mandir, a prominent temple dedicated to Sita. Built in 1874 according to the Nepal tourism board, the three-storey structure is known for its blend of Mughal and local architectural styles. It is among Nepal’s most important religious landmarks.

The Janki Mandir in Janakpur, Nepal. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

Janakpur is associated with the wedding of Ram and Sita. Every year, the occasion is commemorated during Vivah Panchami, a festival that draws pilgrims from India and Nepal. The Vivah Mandap, near the Janaki Mandir, is traditionally identified as the site of their wedding. The city is also known for its many ponds.

Nepal has been keen to promote Janakpur as an important part of the Ramayana circuit, a network of religious destinations associated with the life of Ram. In December 2023, Nepal’s then Ambassador to India, Shankar Prasad Sharma, described Janakpur as an indispensable part of the circuit and said the two countries were working towards establishing a sister-city relationship between Janakpur and Ayodhya.

Story continues below this ad

Where is Sita’s birthplace?

While some believe Sita’s birthplace to be Janakpur, others regard Punaura Dham, near Sitamarhi in Bihar, as the birthplace.

title: How just one ingredient can make ‘fairness’ creams dangerous for health
content_html:
Fairness creams purchased online often lack ingredient labels. (Magnific)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

A 17-year-old girl from Keralam developed a kidney disease called membranous nephropathy and was hospitalised after she used a so-called fairness cream with alarmingly high levels of mercury.

Keralam Health Minister K Muraleedharan on Sunday (November 22) ordered stringent action against the sale of illegal cosmetic products and protein powders, as well as those who promote them through social media. He also said that some of these creams were coming from Pakistan. Earlier this month, Madhya Pradesh also cracked down on unauthorised Pakistan-made ‘whitening’ creams.

What happened in this case, what makes such creams potentially harmful, and how does the government regulate them?

The Keralam case

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The girl purchased a fairness cream from an e-commerce platform after a vlogger recommended it. After she complained of swelling on the body (edema), bubbly urine and other symptoms, she was taken to the Aster MIMS Hospital at Areekode in Malappuram.

She was then diagnosed with membranous nephropathy, a medical condition in which the immune system damages the glomeruli, or the tiny filtering units of the kidneys. The resulting injury allows proteins, particularly albumin, to escape into urine.

The patient’s history showed that she has been using a fairness cream, whose samples were tested outside the state and found to have high mercury levels. Several people have since shared similar experiences on social media.

Prevalence in Keralam

According to Dr S Gouri, a nephrologist who diagnosed the girl’s case, the Aster MIMS hospital at Kottakkal (in Malappuram district) alone reported 13 similar cases between 2021 and 2023. The patients had purchased creams over the counter or via online platforms.

Story continues below this ad
Also Read | How a fairness cream left a Kerala teenager battling kidney disease

She said nephrologists in the state have been made aware of the issue for the last five years, due to kidney-related ailments caused by high-mercury cosmetics. The issue has also been debated at a state-level conference of nephrologists.

In such cases, recovery may take three months to a year. Dr Gouri said that most patients were young and middle-aged, and none reportedly underwent dialysis. The disease does not turn fatal mainly because of early diagnosis, as the intense symptoms force patients to consult nephrologists.

Why is mercury added to fairness products?

The permitted level of mercury in such cosmetics is 1 ppm, but the mercury content found in this cream’s sample was around 12,500 ppm.

Skin care products sometimes contain mercury, which functions as a lightening agent due to its ability to inhibit melanin production. Melanin is a pigment produced naturally by the body to protect the skin against the sun’s ultraviolet rays, and it results in darker skin and hair colour.

Story continues below this ad
In Express | Toxic beauty: Why Maharashtra FDA’s warning on mercury-laced skin-lightening creams should concern every consumer

Once applied to the skin, mercury inactivates tyrosinase, an enzyme that supports melanin production. Higher tyrosinase activity produces more melanin, resulting in darker skin, while low activity does the reverse. When incorporated in a cream, mercury is easily absorbed into the skin and spreads throughout the body.

According to the US FDA, mercury absorption can cause kidney damage, potentially leading to rapid kidney failure, as well as neurological damage such as tremors, tingling or numbness, headaches, fatigue, and mood or cognitive disturbances.

What rules govern cosmetics in India?

The Union Health Ministry implemented the Cosmetic Rules of 2020 for a separate legal framework for the industry and to protect consumer interests. Cosmetics were earlier under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945.

Section 39 (5) of the Cosmetic Rules fixes the “level of unintentional mercury” in cosmetic products at 1 ppm. For products meant for around the eye, the level should not exceed seventy parts per million (0.007%). The rules also state that product labels should disclose any hazardous or poisonous ingredients, while the inner label must have a statement indicating the exact names and quantities of those ingredients.

Creams purchased online often lack ingredient labels.

Story continues below this ad

Both the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation under the Union Government and state drug control departments have different roles in governing the cosmetics industry. The central body monitors imports, approves new products with novel ingredients, and sets national safety standards, while the state body issues licenses to domestic manufacturers, inspects factories, and monitors retail markets against spurious or unsafe products.

According to Kerala’s drugs control department, a special drive held in July this year against the illegal sale of cosmetic products (mainly fairness creams and lipstick) led to 15 cases being registered and cosmetics worth Rs 4 lakhs being seized. These cases were registered after a raid in the domestic market and most were against traders who sold products without a manufacturing license. High levels of mercury were detected in two fairness creams, with a content of up to 15,000 ppm. Lab reports are awaited for further action.

Since 2025, the department has also conducted awareness drives among higher secondary school students. Across over 334 sessions, with each camp having at least 50 students, students have been made aware of harmful fairness creams and lipsticks containing toxins.

Globally, the Minamata Convention was adopted in 2013 under the United Nations Environmental Programme to protect human life from the health hazards of mercury. Named after the Japanese city of Minamata, where mercury poisoning had been a major issue, the treaty is envisaged to phase out/control the use of mercury in consumer/skin care products, among other objectives.

Story continues below this ad

Article 4 of the convention requires all parties not to allow the manufacture, import or export of cosmetics (with mercury content above 1ppm), including skin lightening soaps and creams. India ratified the convention in 2018.

title: Why SC issued notice to Centre and CJI over appointments of judges
content_html:
The Supreme Court last week issued notice to the Union government and the Chief Justice of India (CJI) in a public interest litigation by the NGO Lok Prahari seeking directions to finalise the revised Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) for appointing judges to the Supreme Court and the High Courts.

The plea argues that the revision has remained pending since December 2015, when a Constitution Bench left the task to the Centre after striking down the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC).

Advertisement

Here’s what to know about the case, what the MoP is, and what happened in the 2015 case concerning the NJAC and since then.

What is the case?

A bench of Justices M M Sundresh and P B Varale issued notice to the Centre and to the Supreme Court itself. In its administrative capacity, the court must respond to the plea on MoP and also bring Collegium decisions within the Right to Information (RTI) Act. 

Justice Sundresh, who is a member of the Supreme Court Collegium, first asked the counsel if there were any objections to him hearing the case. Senior Advocate Sanjay Hegde, appearing for the petitioner, told the bench that many judges would be Collegium members and that the objection would always remain, after which the court issued notice. 

Advertisement
Also in Explained | Collegium vs NJAC: What is the renewed debate over appointment of judges?

Earlier, the case had first come up on November 2 before a bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe. Justice Narasimha recused himself because he had earlier appeared as an Additional Solicitor General in the NJAC proceedings.

What is the Memorandum of Procedure?

The MoP is the document that sets out the steps for the appointment, elevation, and transfer of judges of the High Courts and the Supreme Court. A set of mutually agreed-upon conventions, it was first drawn up on June 30, 1999, following the Second Judges case (1993) and the Third Judges case (1998), in which the Supreme Court gave the Collegium of senior judges primacy in appointments.

The CJI initiates proposals for Supreme Court appointments, while the Chief Justice of a High Court, in consultation with the two senior-most puisne judges, initiates proposals for that High Court. The timeline and the process are laid out in the MoP. As per the Law Ministry’s responses to queries in Parliament, the process of appointment of judges continues to be governed by the 1999 MoP.

What happened in the 2015 NJAC case?

On October 16, 2015, a five-judge Constitution Bench declared the 99th Constitutional Amendment — which sought to establish the NJAC for appointing and transferring judges in India’s higher judiciary — unconstitutional, restoring the Collegium system. The NJAC would comprise a six-member panel comprising the CJI, two senior judges, the Law Minister, and two eminent persons.

In the same order, it listed the case to consider measures for improving the working of the Collegium. The court received suggestions running to about 11,500 pages, which were compiled under four heads: transparency, a Collegium secretariat, eligibility criteria, and complaints.

During the hearings, then Attorney General Mukul Rohatgi submitted that drafting the MoP was an executive function, and pointed to the Second Judges case, which had left the drafting of the MoP to the government in consultation with the CJI. The bench accepted his submission and in its order of December 16, 2015, said the government “may finalise the existing Memorandum of Procedure by supplementing it in consultation with the Chief Justice of India”, and that the CJI would decide based on the unanimous view of the Collegium.

Also read | A lesser evil: Collegium has grave deficiencies, but it compromises structural independence of judiciary less

The order also set out the factors to be taken into account: eligibility criteria such as minimum age; publication of the criteria and procedure on the websites of the courts and the Department of Justice; a procedure for minuting Collegium discussions, including dissenting opinions; a secretariat for the Supreme Court and each High Court; and a mechanism to deal with complaints against candidates. The court described these as “broad suggestions” and did not fix a time limit.

What has happened since?

Until 2017, broad consultations continued between the government and the Supreme Court. Although the fine print of the draft was never made publicly available, it was reported that a draft MoP was first sent to the judiciary in March 2016. It is learnt that the Supreme Court did not yield on two key aspects: that the Centre should have the power to reject a name on grounds of “national security”, and a proposal for a permanent secretariat for the Collegium. 

A parliamentary standing committee chaired by Anand Sharma had said in December 2016 that the lack of consensus between the executive and the judiciary on the MoP was delaying appointments. On July 11, 2017, after the Supreme Court’s judgment in the contempt case against Calcutta High Court judge C S Karnan noted the need to revisit the selection process, the government wrote to the Supreme Court’s Secretary General about improving the draft. However, there was no movement on the MoP. 

In 2023, then Union Law Minister Kiren Rijiju had written to then CJI D Y Chandrachud, suggesting that a search-cum-evaluation committee for Supreme Court judges and High Court Chief Justices include a nominee of the Centre, and that committees for High Court judges include nominees of both the Centre and the state government.

The letter raised questions about whether the government is making a fresh legislative move to replace the collegium system for appointing judges. However, within days, the government, in a written reply to the Rajya Sabha, underlined that it was only a suggestion to act as a “facilitator” and that the Collegium would retain the final decision to recommend judges. 

Once again, the issue was not brought up. 

Also read | Collegium system is better than the NJAC
The Supreme Court has sought responses from the Centre and its Secretary General on a plea seeking finalisation of the revised MoP for appointing judges.

On the secretariat issue, the Supreme Court over the years seems to have accepted the suggestion. The Collegium, through successive CJIs, established a system looking at data and the performance of judges, with continuous logs being maintained. 

On the “national security veto”, although the government has not formally pressed it, there are several instances where the government has, in effect, exercised a veto or simply refused to make an appointment despite the Supreme Court Collegium reiterating its recommendation. For example, in the case of the Collegium’s recommendation that Senior Advocate Saurabh Kirpal be appointed as judge of the Delhi High Court, the government had enlisted the Research & Analysis Wing to raise questions of his homosexuality and his partner’s Swiss nationality. 

What has the Supreme Court done so far?

In October 2017, a bench of Justices A K Goel and U U Lalit sought the Centre’s response on the delay in a petition by advocate R P Luthra, observing that although no time limit had been fixed, the issue could not remain pending indefinitely. The case was later listed before a bench headed by then CJI Dipak Misra, which recalled that order.

In RTI responses to the petitioner, it is learnt that the MoP as finalised by the Collegium was sent to the government in March 2017 and that the matter was “under consideration”. The Department of Justice (under the Law Ministry) has declined other requests on the ground that the information is classified and under consideration of constitutional authorities. In February 2026, Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal told the Rajya Sabha that “the process to revise the MoP was under consideration and that further steps would follow once it was complete”.

What happens next?

The Centre and the Secretary General of the Supreme Court will file their responses before the matter is heard again.

title: Bisleri water case: The chemicals, conflicting safety tests and Reliance angle
content_html:
The Rs 30,000 crore bottled water segment in India is dominated by players like Parle Products’ Bisleri, Coca-Cola’s Kinley, and PepsiCo’s Aquafina.
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

India’s apex food safety regulator, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), on Monday (November 22) announced enforcement action against nine entities — including ‘sanction of prosecution’ for India’s largest bottled water manufacturer, Bisleri.

‘Sanction of prosecution’, under Section 42 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, refers to the official approval required from the Commissioner of Food Safety before criminal legal proceedings can be launched against an offender.

The move comes after a fresh round of inspections and compliance verifications. Here is what is known so far.

What is the case against Bisleri?

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

In a social media post, the FSSAI said that the regulatory sample of “Packaged Drinking Water (other than Mineral Water)” was collected from the premises of M/s Bisleri International Pvt. Ltd. for analysis, and the sample was found “non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under the FSS Act, 2006”.

“Upon appeal by the FBO (Food Business Operator), the sample was referred to the Referral Food Laboratory, which also declared it unsafe due to the detection of polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). The laboratory findings established violations relating to unsafe food under the FSS Act, 2006. Sanction has been granted to launch prosecution under the FSS Act, 2006, against M/s Bisleri International Pvt. Ltd,” the regulator said.

What risk do bromate and PAHs pose?

According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), the chemical compound is not typically present in natural raw water at high levels; rather, it primarily forms as a disinfection by-product during drinking-water treatment processes.

Exposure to bromate carries several significant health risks, categorised by toxicity and long-term carcinogenic potential.

Story continues below this ad
Also Read | The Bisleri scare: What excess chemicals found by FSSAI do to your body

High-dose ingestion causes severe gastrointestinal distress (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea), central nervous system depression, hemolytic anaemia (a disorder involving destruction of red blood cells), and pulmonary edema (excessive fluid in the lungs), according to the WHO.

Further, severe acute poisoning can result in irreversible renal failure and deafness/hearing loss. Animal studies demonstrate that elevated bromate intake leads to severe kidney and liver toxicity, evidenced by marked increases in blood urea nitrogen and liver enzymes, as well as kidney tissue lesions.

Polynuclear Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs) are chemicals that occur naturally in coal, crude oil, and gasoline, and are produced when coal, oil, gas, wood, garbage, and tobacco are burned, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency.

What has Bisleri argued?

In its statement, the company said, “We are aware of recent media reports that the FSSAI has issued a notice to Bisleri. The matter dates back approximately 14 months, to a batch produced in September 2025 at Bisleri’s Goa manufacturing facility, one of 143 plants in our network.

Story continues below this ad

On September 30, 2025, FSSAI collected six samples from the Goa facility. Initial testing found that five samples met all applicable standards. The sixth recorded a bromate level of 12 micrograms per litre, against the prescribed limit of 10 micrograms per litre.”

Following Bisleri’s appeal dated November 22, 2025, the FSSAI sent that sample to a referral laboratory for retesting. The referral laboratory found bromate levels to be within the prescribed limit and separately flagged PAHs in the sample.

Bisleri said the difference between the two results raised questions and warranted clarification. It arranged for the same sample to be tested independently at an FSSAI-approved laboratory. That test found bromate within the prescribed limit, the company said.

“We submitted the independent test results to FSSAI’s Western Regional Office with a formal letter dated 2 February 2026. We received no further communication from FSSAI after that submission and understood the matter to be closed,” the company said.

Story continues below this ad

“To date, Bisleri has received no notice by email or in hard copy and has been unable to locate the reported notice on FSSAI’s website. Drinking water safety is a priority for Bisleri. We maintain stringent quality controls of over 90 tests across our 10-step manufacturing process and will continue to cooperate with FSSAI to address the matter through the appropriate regulatory process. A trusted brand for years, Bisleri remains safe for consumption,” Bisleri said in a statement.

Timing of FSSAI inspection

Bisleri said the enforcement action was announced on Monday, but the issue dates back to last year. As per the company, it did not receive any notices in recent months and considered the “matter closed”.

The sample collection also came amid changes within the sector. It happened days before Reliance Consumer Products, the FMCG unit of Reliance Industries, was set to launch its new packaged water product called Campa Sure in October 2025. Campa Sure’s launch was scheduled just days after the government’s September 22 decision to reduce tax on packaged water to 5% from 18% as part of a broader rate rationalisation plan covering multiple product groups.

Reliance Consumer Products in June 2025 also announced plans to invest up to Rs 8,000 crore over 12-15 months to expand beverage manufacturing. The Rs 30,000 crore bottled water segment in India is dominated by players like Parle Products’ Bisleri, Coca-Cola’s Kinley, and PepsiCo’s Aquafina.

Story continues below this ad

Bisleri reported annual sales of $345.31 million for the year ending March 2025, as per Reuters, and had also launched the product in the UAE last year, saying, “The region offers significant growth opportunities, driven by a large Indian diaspora familiar with our brands.”
