title: Why Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO
content_html:
Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO following the board's decision to reinstate him on November 23, 2026. (NYT)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Less than two weeks after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia amid revelations about his extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, the chipmaker’s board has unanimously voted to reinstate him.

Nvidia announced on Monday (November 23) that Huang would return as president, CEO and board member, reversing its earlier refusal to consider his reinstatement despite mounting pressure from US President Donald Trump, Silicon Valley executives and investors.

“Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA,” board chairman Harvey Jones said, adding that his reinstatement was in the best interests of the company’s shareholders, employees, partners and customers.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Trump, who had repeatedly called for Huang’s return, welcomed the reversal on Truth Social. “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” he wrote.

Nvidia shares surged more than 30% in premarket trading following the announcement, according to Reuters. Huang, meanwhile, said he was “honored to return” and thanked the board, employees and supporters for their confidence.

Why did Trump push for Huang’s return?

Despite reportedly being informed twice by his advisers about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy, Trump has publicly expressed his support of the former Nvidia CEO and called him a “legend” in a social media post following his resignation.

The two have had a seemingly symbiotic relationship, with Trump seeing Nvidia as “essentially too big to fail”, according to a November 12 investigation by The New York Times. Nvidia’s success has been integral to the US’s continued position as the market leader in artificial intelligence, a sector central to Trump’s economic agenda.

Story continues below this ad

The NYT also reported that Trump saw Huang as a modern-day Henry Ford who was leading a technological revolution, and that he viewed the company’s fortunes as closely intertwined with those of the US economy and stock market. Trump was concerned that Huang’s removal could trigger an economic downturn.

More Explained | Jensen Huang’s scandal exposes Nvidia’s ‘key-man risk’. What does it mean?

Trump also has a personal financial stake in Nvidia: an analysis of his financial disclosures by The Washington Post found that he held between $13 million and $62 million worth of the chipmaker’s shares as of the end of August.

According to The NYT, Trump even called Huang on November 10, shortly before his resignation, and urged him to keep fighting for his job.

Huang’s friendship with Trump developed during the president’s second term, when Huang and his wife Lori attended a donor dinner at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago residence in April 2025. That month, Nvidia announced plans to produce up to $500 billion worth of AI infrastructure in the US over four years. The White House hailed the announcement as the “Trump effect”, linking it to the Trump’s efforts to revive American manufacturing.

Story continues below this ad

Huang was soon invited to accompany the US President on his visit to West Asia, where major deals involving Nvidia chips were announced.

Huang also successfully lobbied to ease restrictions on advanced American chip sales to China, despite objections from senior administration officials. He argued that wider adoption of US technology would help America maintain its lead over China in AI. The administration subsequently permitted certain Nvidia chip sales to China, drawing criticism over national security risks.

Who else is on Team Huang?

Elon Musk (left) and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the US-Saudi Investment Forum in Washington on November 19, 2025. (Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times)

Elon Musk has warned that Nvidia could lose important business relationships following Huang’s departure.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Musk wrote on X. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

Story continues below this ad

Huang himself has spoken about the importance of such relationships. In an interview earlier this year, he said Nvidia had worked with chipmaker TSMC for nearly three decades without a legal contract, with the two companies relying on mutual trust.

Fortnite-maker Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Replit CEO Amjad Masad have also backed Huang’s reinstatement. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called Huang “a personal hero of mine”, but declined to take a position on whether he should return, saying he did not know enough about the matter.

Also in Explained | Behind Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair lies a much bigger China controversy

The campaign has also drawn support from prominent Nvidia investors. In an open letter to the company’s board, Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker urged directors to keep “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang”.

Why is Nvidia’s board opposed to Huang’s return as CEO?

Huang said last week he would be honoured to return if the board considered it in the best interests of shareholders and employees. However, Nvidia has maintained that he resigned following disclosures of behaviour inconsistent with its code of conduct and standards.

Story continues below this ad

At the company’s earnings call on November 17, chairman Harvey Jones said: “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

The company’s independent investigation remains underway, while long-serving CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO.

The board has also established a committee to oversee national security and export-control compliance, as scrutiny grows over Nvidia’s dealings with China. Kress has sought to reassure investors that the company’s relationships with major customers and suppliers remain intact.

The concerns extend beyond corporate governance. On Sunday (November 22), The NYT reported that US intelligence had tracked Alice Huang’s contacts with China’s Ministry of State Security during her relationship with Jensen Huang. US authorities are also investigating whether advanced Nvidia chips obtained by companies connected to her were illegally diverted to China.

Story continues below this ad

The US Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating whether Nvidia’s disclosures misled investors, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The controversy has divided investors over whether Huang’s return would restore confidence or expose the company to further risks. An institutional Nvidia shareholder, speaking anonymously to Reuters, expressed reservations about reinstating him before the investigations concluded, pointing to Apple and Microsoft as examples of companies that continued to prosper after the departure of influential leaders.

The divisions extend to the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent previously called for an outside successor and criticised the Commerce Department’s handling of chip exports to China. On Sunday (November 22), he said the US government was seeking answers about Nvidia’s chip sales to China and who had overseen compliance under Huang’s leadership.

title: ‘Token Factory operates on GPUs procured privately’: Sarvam’s defence amid Chinese AI models row
content_html:
Indian artificial intelligence (AI) startup Sarvam has defended its decision to offer Chinese-developed AI models through its newly launched Token Factory platform, clarifying that the service runs on privately procured computing infrastructure without government subsidies.

This comes amid questions over whether the company’s commercial strategy is at odds with India’s ambitions to build indigenous AI capabilities and reduce its dependence on foreign technologies.

Advertisement

The controversy has brought into focus a fundamental tension in India’s sovereign AI push, in that whether technological sovereignty should mean developing powerful AI models domestically, or ensuring that the infrastructure on which they operate, and the data they process, remain under Indian control, irrespective of where the models originate.

Sarvam’s position is particularly significant because it is among the most prominent startups selected under the government’s Rs 10,370 crore IndiaAI Mission to develop homegrown foundation models. Its decision to offer models from Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba and Z.ai has therefore raised questions about the commercial viability of India’s pursuit of technological self-reliance.

What Sarvam said about Token Factory

In a post on social media platform X, Sarvam co-founder Pratyush Kumar said the IndiaAI Mission, under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), had provided around 20 startups subsidised access to graphics processing units (GPUs), offering a 40% discount on computing costs. He said Sarvam used this support to train its proprietary Sarvam 105B model from scratch, which was completed and open-sourced in February.

Advertisement

“The government did not pay Sarvam directly, instead like with every supported startup, the subsidy went to GPU cloud providers, helping seed AI infra in the country,” he said.

Kumar maintained that Token Factory, which offers several foreign-developed open-weight models, operates on GPUs procured privately by Sarvam, without government support. He also argued that the growing adoption of open-weight AI models globally had created an opportunity for Indian enterprises to access powerful AI systems at lower costs, while retaining greater control over their technology infrastructure.

“Sarvam Token Factory is one of the first large inference offerings in India. We serve multiple open-weight models on GPUs we have privately procured, without any government support. We have optimised datacenter scale inference to make our token cost comparable to or lower than established providers such as Fireworks, Baseten and Together,” Kumar said.

However, Indian businesses often face data residency requirements and need low-latency AI services, making reliance on overseas inference providers challenging.

“Today, India consumes a few trillion tokens a day and imports the majority of them,” Kumar said, arguing that investments in domestic computing infrastructure were essential to reduce this dependence.

Kumar rejected suggestions that offering foreign models conflicted with Sarvam’s long-term objective of developing indigenous AI systems. “Building inference capability does not conflict with our core mission: training our own models,” he said.

He announced an improved version of the company’s proprietary model, Sarvam 105B-1711, which he claimed offers better reasoning, tool-calling and collaborative task capabilities, particularly in Indian languages, at an output cost of Rs 25 per million tokens.

Sarvam also plans to release models for vision, speech and edge AI over the next two weeks, while working with partners to bring advanced computing infrastructure into India.

Acknowledging that developing globally competitive AI systems requires investments running into hundreds of millions, and eventually billions, of dollars, Kumar said Sarvam intended to build a commercially sustainable inference business alongside its indigenous model development efforts.

The strategy underscores the larger challenge confronting India’s sovereign AI ambitions, which is building commercially viable AI businesses today while investing in the expensive, long-term effort of reducing dependence on foreign-developed foundation models.

“We firmly believe that India can and must win across the full-stack of AI,” Kumar said.

What is Sarvam’s Token Factory?

Sarvam’s Token Factory is an AI inference platform that allows businesses to run different AI models using Sarvam’s computing infrastructure located in India.

Inference platforms are services that allow businesses and developers to run AI models without having to purchase expensive computing hardware or manage the infrastructure themselves. While developing and training an AI model requires substantial investment, running it at scale also demands considerable computing resources.

Inference providers offer access to different AI models through application programming interfaces (APIs), typically charging customers based on the number of tokens processed. This allows businesses to choose models suited to specific tasks without being tied to a single developer, while benefiting from economies of scale and optimised computing infrastructure.

The model is well established globally, with companies such as Together AI, Fireworks AI and DeepInfra providing inference services for models developed by other firms. OpenRouter, another prominent player, offers developers access to hundreds of AI models, routing requests to different inference providers. Technology giants such as Amazon also offer similar capabilities through platforms such as AWS Bedrock, which allows enterprises to access models from multiple developers.

Sarvam is offering models such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM 5.3 and Qwen 3.8 27B, alongside its own Sarvam 105B model. Some are available on demand, while others require dedicated capacity.

The company claims that it is already serving more than 450 billion tokens daily through DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, indicating the substantial scale at which it is running the Chinese-developed model.

However, Indian businesses often face data residency requirements and need low-latency AI services, making reliance on overseas inference providers challenging.
“Today, India consumes a few trillion tokens a day and imports the majority of them,” Kumar said, arguing that investments in domestic computing infrastructure were essential to reduce this dependence.
Kumar rejected suggestions that offering foreign models conflicted with Sarvam’s long-term objective of developing indigenous AI systems. “Building inference capability does not conflict with our core mission: training our own models,” he said.
He announced an improved version of the company’s proprietary model, Sarvam 105B-1711, which he claimed offers better reasoning, tool-calling and collaborative task capabilities, particularly in Indian languages, at an output cost of Rs 25 per million tokens.
Sarvam also plans to release models for vision, speech and edge AI over the next two weeks, while working with partners to bring advanced computing infrastructure into India.
Acknowledging that developing globally competitive AI systems requires investments running into hundreds of millions, and eventually billions, of dollars, Kumar said Sarvam intended to build a commercially sustainable inference business alongside its indigenous model development efforts.
The strategy underscores the larger challenge confronting India’s sovereign AI ambitions, which is building commercially viable AI businesses today while investing in the expensive, long-term effort of reducing dependence on foreign-developed foundation models.
“We firmly believe that India can and must win across the full-stack of AI,” Kumar said.
What is Sarvam’s Token Factory?
Sarvam’s Token Factory is an AI inference platform that allows businesses to run different AI models using Sarvam’s computing infrastructure located in India.
Inference platforms are services that allow businesses and developers to run AI models without having to purchase expensive computing hardware or manage the infrastructure themselves. While developing and training an AI model requires substantial investment, running it at scale also demands considerable computing resources.
Inference providers offer access to different AI models through application programming interfaces (APIs), typically charging customers based on the number of tokens processed. This allows businesses to choose models suited to specific tasks without being tied to a single developer, while benefiting from economies of scale and optimised computing infrastructure.
The model is well established globally, with companies such as Together AI, Fireworks AI and DeepInfra providing inference services for models developed by other firms. OpenRouter, another prominent player, offers developers access to hundreds of AI models, routing requests to different inference providers. Technology giants such as Amazon also offer similar capabilities through platforms such as AWS Bedrock, which allows enterprises to access models from multiple developers.
Sarvam is offering models such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM 5.3 and Qwen 3.8 27B, alongside its own Sarvam 105B model. Some are available on demand, while others require dedicated capacity.
The company claims that it is already serving more than 450 billion tokens daily through DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, indicating the substantial scale at which it is running the Chinese-developed model.

title: FPI disclosure relief: Why SEBI wants to ease rules, and could it reduce transparency?
content_html:
SEBI has proposed easing disclosure requirements for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) to attract foreign capital, raising questions about transparency and beneficial ownership in Indian markets. (Magnific)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Three years after proposing stringent disclosure norms, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) on Friday proposed to make the Indian markets more attractive for foreign investors by scrapping additional disclosure requirements linked to concentration and size.

The regulator said current rules in this regard are more stringent than in competing markets. This means these foreign players won’t now have to report every single detail when holding an Indian company’s shares, but does the proposed relaxation come at the cost of market integrity? Also, the proposed relaxation raises questions about transparency and the ability to identify the ultimate beneficiaries behind large foreign investments.

While SEBI’s objective is to reduce regulatory friction and attract foreign capital, the trade-off could be reduced granular transparency in the case of some of the foreign funds. The challenge for the regulator will be to ensure that easing compliance does not create greater opacity in India’s capital markets or compromise safeguards against money laundering, regulatory circumvention and the concealment of beneficial ownership, market sources said.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What changes has SEBI proposed to FPI disclosure rules?

A day after SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said it will release a consultation paper to simplify regulatory frameworks for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs), the regulator released a paper proposing to scrap detailed disclosure norms for foreign players.

Currently, certain FPIs have to disclose detailed information about all entities invested in them under the additional disclosure framework (ADF), including individual investors, irrespective of the size of their holdings. This granular disclosure applies to foreign funds with more than half of their Indian portfolio in a single corporate group, or to FPIs that, individually or with their investor group, hold more than Rs 50,000 crore worth of Indian equities.

Also in Explained | FPIs pump record $11.3 billion in November: What drove this comeback?

SEBI says these requirements have imposed considerable compliance costs, forcing global funds to undertake extensive investor identification exercises, sometimes establish separate vehicles for Indian investments and repeatedly update disclosures as investors enter or exit pooled funds. Complex structures such as fund-of-funds arrangements have also made compliance particularly difficult.

The regulator now proposes to remove this ADF altogether for FPIs, with an aim to make regulations in the Indian market comparable to other major markets. The regulator has kept the proposal open for public comments till December 11.

Story continues below this ad

Why did SEBI tighten FPI disclosure norms after the Hindenburg-Adani controversy?

The ADF was introduced in August 2023, in the aftermath of the Hindenburg report on the Adani Group. The controversy had raised questions about whether certain offshore FPIs were being used to conceal the true beneficial ownership of shares and potentially circumvent minimum public shareholding requirements.

The Supreme Court-appointed expert committee had subsequently noted that SEBI’s investigation into the ownership of offshore entities investing in Adani stocks faced difficulties in establishing the ultimate ownership of several FPIs. The committee noted that information sought from regulators in foreign jurisdictions had not been forthcoming.

The ADF was brought into effect to prevent opaque offshore corporate structures from escaping Indian authorities after the controversy between US research firm Hindenburg and the Adani Group but exempts FPI categories like foreign government-driven or sovereign funds, foreign public retail funds, and entities listed in foreign markets.

SEBI then dropped allegations that offshore funds had been effectively controlled by Adani and were being used to breach minimum public shareholding norms in four Adani companies.

Story continues below this ad
Also Read | Why have gold prices fallen by 25% in nine months, and could they dip further?

This makes SEBI’s latest proposal politically and regulatorily sensitive. The very framework that emerged amid concerns over opacity in offshore shareholding structures is now proposed to be dismantled.

Why does SEBI want to ease disclosure requirements for foreign investors?

According to the regulator, the ADF was more of a compliance burden on foreign investors than a security measure. “Disclosure requirements that are not in line with globally accepted practices could potentially place India at a competitive disadvantage vis-à-vis peer jurisdictions with relatively lenient regulatory requirements,” SEBI wrote in its consultation paper.

“Many foreign investors looking to invest in India consider the granular disclosure requirements as an additional compliance burden. Rather than investing in India and being subject to granular disclosures, many investors may instead choose to avoid investing in India,” it added. The regulator also argued that existing provisions like the restrictions under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) and the Press Note 2 issued in March already cover the purpose of the ADF.

“This is positive. It is not going to fully deliver on our expectations, but it is definitely positive. It will widen the participation of FPIs in the market. But actual momentum and flow will depend upon, you know, the relative valuation, the economic growth story, corporate earnings, all that,” said G Chokkalingam, founder of Equinomics Research. “I don’t think this is going to be negative or compromised. You know, it doesn’t stop SEBI from investigating any individual cases,” he said.

Story continues below this ad

The proposal does not mean beneficial ownership disclosures will disappear altogether. FPIs would still be subject to the applicable beneficial ownership identification requirements under the Prevention of Money Laundering Rules. But removing the ADF would eliminate the additional, threshold-triggered, full-look-through disclosure obligation.

Could relaxing FPI disclosure rules reduce market transparency?

FPIs, particularly those operating through multi-layered offshore structures, pooled funds and jurisdictions with limited disclosure, can make it difficult to establish who ultimately controls capital flowing into Indian companies. Removing the additional layer of disclosures could weaken the visibility of ownership chains, especially in cases involving concentrated holdings or large investment positions.

FPIs, particularly those operating through multi-layered offshore structures, pooled funds and jurisdictions with limited disclosure, can make it difficult to establish who ultimately controls capital flowing into Indian companies. Removing the additional layer of disclosures could weaken the visibility of ownership chains, especially in cases involving concentrated holdings or large investment positions, according to market sources.

Also Read | Blue-chip stocks have performed poorly all year. How did they make a comeback?

SEBI had tightened disclosures in 2023 partly because of concerns that opaque offshore investment structures could undermine genuine public shareholding and market transparency. “Now, it argues that the additional disclosure regime is burdensome, internationally out of step and potentially discouraging foreign capital,” said an analyst.

Story continues below this ad

Will easing disclosure norms attract more foreign investment into India?

While FPIs have bought a record $13 billion worth of Indian shares in November, concerns still remain about whether the flows will remain positive if global conditions worsen again, especially after heavy selling in previous months had been a big headwind for the Indian market. Between October 2024 and October 2026, FPIs pulled out more than $ 60 billion from Indian equities, adding pressure on the rupee and markets amid the West Asia war, Ai disruption, high crude prices and interest rate worries.

The relaxed regulations certainly reduce the compliance burden for FPIs, making regulations comparable to major markets like the US and other emerging economies. However, it is only one factor in the grand scheme of things, and foreign flows depend on other factors like geopolitical conditions, earnings growth, and valuations.

title: Balendra Shah visits India: What is on the table, from security to AI to cricket
content_html:
Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah, popularly known as Balen Shah, is in India on his first bilateral visit abroad since taking office in March. He will meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi for bilateral talks on Monday, in their first in-person meeting.

Nepal’s Prime Ministers generally make their first visit to India, and quite early in their tenure. Yet, much is unusual about this visit, starting with the PM himself.

Advertisement

‘Nepal first’ PM

The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician Balen Shah came to power on the back of massive youth protests, promising a break from Nepal’s old politics of patronage and dependence on regional big powers.

Shah was known for his administrative skills and development work as the Kathmandu Mayor. After taking the top office, in an effort to project difference from the old guard, Shah told ministers and officials to focus on domestic issues. He went so far as to issue a diktat: no foreign visits and no meetings with senior officials and ministers from other countries, unless with a President or a Prime Minister.

Thus, when US envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor visited Kathmandu in April-early May, Shah’s office did not schedule a meeting with him. Around the same time, the visit of India’s Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri to Kathmandu was cancelled as Shah did not agree to a meeting.

Advertisement

Then, Shah said both India and Nepal had encroached on each other’s territory, and sought the involvement of China and UK to address the dispute, something India strongly rejected.

Also in Explained | History of India and Nepal’s border issue

The June visit of Shishir Khanal, Nepal’s Foreign Minister, and Rabi Lamichhane, the chief of Shah’s party, Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), smoothened matters and paved the way for Shah’s visit. His visit is being seen as an acknowledgement in Nepal of the need for continued engagement with India.

The strategic logic for engagement is clear as daylight: India is Nepal’s largest trade, transit and investment partner, Nepal enjoys duty-free access to the Indian market, and India is Nepal’s biggest export destination, receiving about 80% of Nepal’s goods exports. India is also the largest source of foreign investment in Nepal, accounting for almost 1/3rd of the total FDI received by the country.

Thus, even as Shah seeks to differentiate himself from his predecessors, there are key areas of cooperation which India and Nepal will look at.

Key areas of economic cooperation between India and Nepal

Energy: Bilateral cooperation in the power sector has been on an upward trajectory, with developments like the agreement for long term power trade that envisages the import of up to 10,000 MW power from Nepal to India over a period of 10 years. India currently imports about 1200 MW of power from Nepal annually.

Indian entities are involved in the development of several hydropower projects in Nepal, including the 900 MW Arun-3 Hydroelectric project under construction.

Energy supplies to Nepal were made more efficient and effective through a cross-border petroleum pipeline commissioned in 2019 between Motihari and Amlekhgunj. Phase-2 of this pipeline has also been implemented. Both sides are now exploring the development of new pipelines and terminals, and Balen Shah’s visit will look into this aspect.

Innovation ecosystem and AI: With Shah representing the youth, the start-up culture is a major area that India is likely to focus on.

Since 2025, several Nepali startups have received training through the India-Nepal Startup Partnership Network (IN-SPAN) in collaboration with IIT Madras and its Incubation Centre Pravartak.

Both sides are working to establish a collaborative framework for advancing Language AI, digital public infrastructure, and inclusive digital ecosystems across India and Nepal.

Education: For the first few decades after Indian independence, a majority of Nepal’s senior leaders were educated at Banaras Hindu University (BHU). But in recent years, Nepal’s youngsters are choosing Australia, Europe, Thailand, Singapore, and Dubai.

Scholarships provided by India for Nepali nationals provide extensive coverage, from school education to the Doctorate level, with 1,500 annual scholarships.

With Shah seen as the voice of the youth, the Indian government and Nepal are looking at the possibility of an IIT campus in Nepal.

Sports: Cricket has found huge enthusiasm among the Nepalese youth. In the past three years, there has been growth in the India-Nepal partnership in sports cooperation, particularly in cricket. In fact, the Nepal Premier League is said to be a huge money spinner, next to India’s IPL.

Tourism: India is the largest source of foreign tourists to Nepal. The data of air arrivals in the last Nepali financial year reflected 311,000 Indian visitors. This does not include the large number of visitors arriving by road. Both sides are thus working to promote shared circuits such as the Ramayana Circuit and the Buddhist Circuit.

The new direct passenger train services between Janakpurdham and Ayodhya, whose trial run was on November 5, will further facilitate religious tourism between India and Nepal.

India and Nepal already enjoy extensive cooperation in culture. Indian pilgrims visit Pashupatinath, Muktinath, Janaki Mandir and Lumbini, while Nepali pilgrims travel to Kashi, the Char Dham, Bodh Gaya and the Kumbh.

India-Nepal border management question

The most challenging issue during the visit is likely to be border management. While India and Nepal have contested some border areas for decades, in 2020, under former prime minister KP Oli, Nepal officially issued a new political map, showing Kalapani, Limpiadhura and Lipulekh in Uttarakhand as its territory. This locks all Nepal’s Prime Ministers in a position they find difficult to walk back from. Also, China has long sought a larger influence in Nepal, including over its boundary issues.

However, despite the differences, India and Nepal enjoy robust ties in defence and security. With the issue of Agniveers being resolved — by giving them a pathway for permanent commission — some misgivings among the Gorkha soldiers have been assuaged. India and Nepal also cooperate closely in areas such as countering narcotics, cross-border crimes, money laundering etc.

Balen Shah’s visit to India will be a key moment for a reset in the relationship. The effort is to bring the ties back on track, with a new PM who has been vocal about not being “pro-India” or “pro-China”, but “pro-Nepal”. The political establishment in Nepal is new and different from what India has dealt with, but their aspirational and ambitious political language is what India speaks, and well understands.

title: How India’s first indigenous bird flu vaccine was developed, why it matters
content_html:
The bird flu vaccine, which costs Rs 1-2 per dose, was announced by Union Agriculture Minister and former Madhya Pradesh chief minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan in Bhopal on Friday. Photo: PTI
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

For years, India has dealt with recurring outbreaks of bird flu, caused by the highly pathogenic H5N1 strain of avian influenza. While the disease has primarily affected poultry, the virus has increasingly been detected in other animal species, including tigers, leopards, and other mammals. It has also infected humans, raising concerns about its potential to pose a wider public health threat.

Now, scientists at the ICAR-National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD) in Bhopal have developed India’s first indigenous vaccine against H5N1 for chickens. The vaccine, which costs Rs 1-2 per dose, was announced by Union Agriculture Minister and former Madhya Pradesh chief minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan in Bhopal on Friday (November 20).

We explain why the vaccine was needed, the challenges involved in developing it, and what the trials established.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Why India needed a bird flu vaccine

India’s first bird flu outbreak was reported in 2006 in Navapur, Maharashtra. Since then, the country has recorded more than 500 outbreaks, according to figures shared by Chouhan. Outbreaks have resulted in large-scale deaths and culling of poultry, affecting farmers and the wider poultry industry.

The vaccine targets a particular genetic group of the virus known as H5N1 Clade 2.3.2.1a, which has been responsible for a majority of bird flu outbreaks in Indian chickens since 2011.

A clade is a genetic grouping of viruses that share a common ancestry. H5N1 is the name of the virus subtype, while 2.3.2.1a identifies a particular genetic lineage within it. This is important because influenza viruses continue to change over time, and vaccines need to be suited to the strains circulating in a population.

Also read | Why Maharashtra’s poultry farmers are seeking bird flu vaccination

Dr S Nagarajan, principal scientist at NIHSAD who led the team of scientists involved in the vaccine’s development, told The Indian Express, “These outbreaks have caused huge economic loss to the poultry industry… Hence, the vaccine is important to control the clade 2.3.2.1a H5N1 virus strain to mitigate the economic losses to the farmers and to prevent emergence of a human pandemic virus.”

Story continues below this ad

The concern over this particular clade extends beyond poultry. “Outbreaks involving the same viral group were reported in several mammalian species, including tigers, lions, domestic cats, leopards and jungle cats in 2025,” Nagarajan said. According to him, three human deaths involving H5N1 viruses belonging to the same clade were also reported from Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, and Karnataka.

The vaccine is intended to protect chickens, not humans. Its potential public health benefit lies in reducing the circulation of the virus among birds and, consequently, the opportunities for transmission to people who come into contact with infected poultry.

Challenges in development of the vaccine

The vaccine was developed at ICAR-NIHSAD, an institute in Bhopal specialising in the diagnosis, surveillance, and research of high-risk animal diseases.

The institute has been working on avian influenza for years. Its research includes monitoring the different strains circulating in India, studying how the virus changes, and examining its ability to infect different animal species.

Veterinary officials and other staff engaged in culling of birds in Navapur in Maharashtra’s Nandurbar district in February 2021. Photo: Deepak Joshi

title: Rahul Gandhi on Israel: How defence tech, Kargil war shaped India’s ties
content_html:
Lok Sabha LoP Rahul Gandhi during an open question-and-answer session with students and faculty, at University of Chicago, USA. (@INCIndia/X via PTI Photo)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Lok Sabha Leader of the Opposition and Congress leader Rahul Gandhi spoke this week about India needing to maintain its relationship with Israel due to “strategic reasons”.

Gandhi condemned Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attacks and Israel’s actions against Palestinians, while adding that he supported a “strong relationship” with Israel. “We have strategic interests, including buying the best weapons for our armed forces. But that cannot mean silence on Gaza,” he said.

The comments come at a time when Israel has received global criticism, including from its longstanding ally, the United States. They also differ from the stronger, more critical stance adopted by key members of the Congress Party so far.

India’s foreign policy must be guided by what is good for India.

I support a strong relationship with Israel. We have strategic interests, including buying the best weapons for our armed forces. But that cannot mean silence on Gaza.

I condemn the October 7th attacks and the killing of innocent people. I also condemn what Israel has done in Gaza. One wrong cannot justify another.

We are a nation of 1.5 billion people. No country – Israel, USA, Russia or China – should hold us back from playing our rightful role on the global stage.

India must stand for what it believes in.

— Rahul Gandhi (@RahulGandhi) November 19, 2026

India has historically supported the cause of Palestinian statehood, even as it has, of late, deepened relations with Israel. A key factor in this trajectory is defence ties, and one milestone was the 1999 Kargil War. Over the years, The Indian Express has extensively reported on and explained the history and the shifts. This article brings together those explainers to provide a one-stop guide.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Where India stood on Israel, Palestine historically

As The Indian Express earlier reported on India-Israel ties, India recognised the State of Israel soon after it was created in 1948. The establishment of full diplomatic relations would take four more decades, influenced by how national leaders perceived the issue at the time.

Jawaharlal Nehru and Mahatma Gandhi opposed the creation of a State based on religion — a view in line with their opposition to the Partition of India. India’s position with regard to Palestine was also guided by the consensus in the Arab world, the Non-Aligned Movement, and the United Nations.

On January 10, 1975, India recognised the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) as the sole and legitimate representative of the Palestinian people and permitted it an independent office in New Delhi.

Also Read | Mahatma Gandhi’s views on Israel, Palestine

Notably, this stance was retained during the first non-Congress government at the Centre in 1977, led by the Janata Party. Addressing a public meeting arranged by the Indo-Arab Friendship League on January 28, 1978, then External Affairs Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee asked the Non-Aligned Movement and all those who believed in peace and justice in the world to “raise their voice in protest against the injustice being meted out to Palestinians”.

Story continues below this ad

India’s changing ties with Israel

Former West Asian studies professor PR Kumaraswamy earlier wrote that over time, factors like the Cold War’s end and the willingness of Arab countries to negotiate peace, as well as India obtaining arms from Israel during the 1962 China War and the Indo-Pakistani wars in 1965 and 1971, hinted at a sense of “shared security” with Israel.

Following his 1984 electoral victory, Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi initiated some contacts with Israel, which “became an integral part of the pragmatic, non-ideological approach to foreign policy pursued by Narasimha Rao.”

As earlier reported, the Arab countries’ neutral position during the 1962 war and their support for Pakistan in later conflicts did not go down well with many, including the BJP. Things changed in West Asia when Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990. The PLO lost its political leverage on account of its support for Saddam Hussein. Around that time, the Soviet Union disintegrated, and this prompted India to make drastic changes in its policy towards West Asia.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was in India on January 19-20, 1992. During a meeting with Prime Minister P V Narasimha Rao, he was told that India’s establishment of the relationship with Israel would be helpful for the Palestinian cause. He was told that New Delhi could exert influence on Israel only if it had an ambassador in Tel Aviv. Arafat came on board.

Story continues below this ad

He then famously told a press conference in New Delhi: “Exchange of Ambassadors and recognition (of Israel) are acts of sovereignty in which I cannot interfere… I respect any choice of the Indian government”. This would prove to be a game-changer. India formally established diplomatic ties with Israel on January 29, 1992, around 10 days after Arafat’s public approval.

The defence factor in India-Israel ties

By the time of the Kargil war in 1999, full diplomatic ties with Israel came in handy. The Indian Air Force (IAF) desperately needed precision bombs to target Pakistani intruders hiding in the caves and bunkers in Kargil’s mountains. After political approvals, IAF leaders reached out to their Israeli counterparts, who wasted no time. Israel is understood to have dug into its emergency stockpiles and shipped them to India’s air bases within days.

Also Read | Israeli help and Indian jugaad in recapture of Tiger Hill

In his visit in 2015 to Israel, then President Pranab Mukherjee had acknowledged and appreciated Israel’s support during the war and thanked it for providing “critical defence supplies”.

India responded to this decisive show of support by organising a series of high-profile visits to Israel in 2000, with external affairs minister Jaswant Singh leading the first-ever Indian bilateral visit to the country. Home Minister L K Advani also visited that summer.

Story continues below this ad

More recently, India has been the biggest purchaser of Israeli weapons over the last decade, especially between 2015 and 2019, including drones, missile systems, sensors, surveillance technology and border-control equipment.

title: Why Cyclone Akvan in Bay of Bengal contributed to early fog in Punjab, Haryana
content_html:
A foggy evening in Hoshiarpur on November 21. (Express photo)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Winters in Punjab are usually dominated by conversations around smog and stubble-burning. This November, however, another winter phenomenon is attracting attention: early fog.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD), Chandigarh, has forecast dense fog at isolated places in Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh from November 19 to 22, weeks before prolonged winter fog normally becomes a regular feature of the northern plains in December and January.

Why is Punjab seeing a foggy November?

Meteorologists attribute the early fog to moisture incursion, light north-westerly winds, atmospheric stability, and night-time cooling. The cyclonic system over the Bay of Bengal is also influencing the larger circulation and moisture pattern.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Fog forms when air near the ground cools to its dew point, the temperature at which moisture in the air condenses to form water droplets. Thus, adequate moisture in the lower atmosphere is as essential as cooling.

Minimum temperatures have been below normal at several locations in Punjab, though the pattern is not uniform. According to IMD Chandigarh observations on November 19, Chandigarh recorded 10.4°C (1°C below normal), Patiala 9.3°C (-2°C), Hisar 10°C (-2°C), Narnaul 9.5°C (-2°C) and Rohtak 10.6°C (-1°C).

This variation is significant because fog is localised: dense patches can form where moisture, surface cooling and weak winds coincide, even as nearby stations record normal or above-normal temperatures.

Also in Explained | Why counting farm fires is not enough to measure the scale of stubble burning

Surinder Pal, director, IMD Chandigarh, said moisture availability, weak winds and falling night temperatures were creating favourable conditions. The IMD’s November 19 bulletin also noted a weak western disturbance, with a trough (an elongated area of relatively low atmospheric pressure) in the middle layers of the atmosphere over eastern Afghanistan and north-west Pakistan.

Story continues below this ad

Why can fog be dense in some areas while nearby areas are clear?

While moisture provides the essential ingredient for fog, light winds and atmospheric stability determine its formation and persistence. Surinder Pal said moisture incursion, along with light north-westerly winds, was creating favourable conditions. Weak winds restrict the mixing and dispersal of air near the surface, allowing moisture to accumulate.

As the ground loses heat through radiation at night, the air above it cools. Once it reaches saturation, water vapour condenses into droplets. Stable atmospheric conditions restrict vertical mixing, allowing radiation fog to develop and persist, particularly during the night and early morning.

Local variations in humidity, irrigation, canals, agricultural fields, vegetation and surface temperatures explain why fog can be dense in isolated locations while nearby areas remain relatively clear.

Is Cyclone Akvan also influencing fog formation in north India?

The Severe Cyclonic Storm Akvan is another factor influencing the prevailing weather pattern. Surinder Pal pointed to its influence on moisture incursion. Cyclonic systems can alter atmospheric circulation and moisture movement over large areas, although Akvan should not be considered the sole or direct cause of fog in Punjab and Haryana.

Story continues below this ad

Is this fog the same as the smog Punjab usually witnesses in November?

No. Fog and smog are different atmospheric phenomena, although they can occur together.
Fog consists of tiny liquid water droplets suspended near the ground, while smog is polluted air containing particulate matter and gases from vehicles, industries and stubble burning. Weak winds and atmospheric stability can trap pollution near the surface, worsening air quality and visibility.

Punjab has frequently witnessed early November smog in recent years, with stubble-burning emissions adding to other sources of pollution. This November, however, the early fog is primarily linked to meteorological conditions, rather than being simply another episode of pollution-induced haze.

The two can coexist. Aerosol particles in polluted air act as cloud condensation nuclei, providing surfaces for water vapour to condense and potentially influencing fog formation and visibility, experts said.
Pal said the early fog does not necessarily signal the start of the prolonged winter fog season. It reflects a temporary convergence of favourable weather conditions, while more persistent fog episodes are usually witnessed in December and January.

title: Why Telangana is scrapping intermediate colleges and merging them with schools
content_html:
The Government City College in Hyderabad. Photo: Wikimedia Commons
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

The Telangana government recently decided to do away with intermediate colleges — also known as junior colleges — and replace them with Classes 11 and 12. From the next academic year (2027-28), the two grades will be integrated into the school system, with existing schools with grades up to Class 10 adding two more and conducting classes.

We explain the rationale behind the state government’s decision and how it will be implemented on the ground.

Why did the Telangana government decide to scrap Intermediate colleges?

A number of students, especially girls, drop out of the education system after passing Class 10. Students, including a majority of those hailing from socially and economically backward communities, complain of the hassle of approaching different junior colleges to get admissions.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The present system takes students through the rules and regulations of two separate education boards: School Education and Intermediate. School education up to Class 10 is managed by the School Education Department and culminates in the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) public examination conducted by the Board of Secondary Education, whereas Intermediate education is governed by the Telangana Board of Intermediate Education. Right to Education and academic activists note that the transition for students to a different type of institution after their Class 10 board exams is difficult and tiresome.

title: Two farmers were caught growing ganja. Why the one who harvested crop faces tougher charge
content_html:
Under the NDPS Act, cultivation of cannabis and possession of ganja attract different penalties, depending on the nature and quantity of the seizure. (Wikimedia Commons)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

On November 17, separate police parties raided two farms in villages 12 km apart in Gujarat’s Rajkot district, following tip-offs that cannabis plants were being grown there.

Growing cannabis without a licence is illegal in Gujarat, and yet some farmers take the risk.

The crop is usually harvested in November and December, keeping the police on alert. The two farmers were booked under different provisions of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act. Here’s why.

The seizures

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

A team from Vinchhiya police station in rural Rajkot raided a farm in Kharachiya Jas village and found seven cannabis plants growing amid cotton on a 2.5-bigha plot belonging to 40-year-old Paba Magan Panchala. The police uprooted the plants and seized 14.45 kg of cannabis valued at Rs 7.225 lakh. They completed the seizure by evening.

About 12 km to the west of Kharachiya Jas, the Special Operations Group (SOG) of the Rajkot Rural Police raided a farm in Chhasiya village of Vinchhiya taluka at 3 pm the same day. But the police completed their panchnama only 15 hours later, at dawn on November 18, after weighing the ganja from plants that 55-year-old Savshi Bachu Mithapara had already harvested on his five-bigha plot of land. The total seizure amounted to 705.49 kg, valued at a whopping Rs 3.52 crore.

Also in Explained | Why growing a cannabis plant in your balcony is a crime, but buying bhang isn’t

Mithapara, who had harvested the cannabis crop just four days before the police raid, was booked for possession of ganja, an offence that carries a maximum prison term of 20 years for commercial quantities. Panchala, meanwhile, was booked for cultivating cannabis, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years, regardless of the number of plants involved.

Why the difference of a decade?

The FIRs in both cases were filed at the same Vinchhiya police station.

Story continues below this ad

Paba Magan Panchala, whose cannabis plants were still standing during the police raid, was booked under Sections 8(b) and 20(a) of the NDPS Act, which prohibit and penalise the cultivation of any cannabis plant. The maximum punishment is 10 years and a fine of up to Rs 1 lakh, regardless of whether the accused cultivated one plant or an entire field.

By contrast, Savshi Bachu Mithapara, who had already harvested his crop, was booked for possession of ganja under Sections 8(c) and 20(b) of the NDPS Act. These provisions cover the production, manufacture, possession, sale, purchase, transport and use of cannabis, among other activities.

Marijuana, or weed, known as ganja in India, consists of the flowering or fruiting tops of the cannabis plant. Under the NDPS Act, seeds and leaves are excluded from this definition when they are not accompanied by these tops.

Since the quantity seized from Mithapara’s field exceeded 20 kg, the threshold for a ‘commercial quantity’ of ganja, the punishment prescribed under Section 20(b)(ii)(C) is rigorous imprisonment of at least 10 years, which may extend to 20 years, along with a fine ranging from Rs 1 lakh to Rs 2 lakh.

Why the condition of the crop matters

Story continues below this ad

There is no difference between the prescribed street value of cannabis plants and ganja decided by the Government of India. According to an October 24, 2025, notification issued by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs, all forms of ganja are valued at Rs 50,000 per kg. This is a fivefold increase from the earlier valuation of Rs 10,000 per kg, police officials confirmed.

Asked why Mithapara had been booked under the more stringent provisions of the NDPS Act despite having cultivated the crop, Inspector Fatehsingh Pargi of the Rajkot Rural SOG told The Indian Express, “The accused Mithapara had cut down the plants and set them out to dry. The number of plants could not even be counted because they had been completely dismantled branches, root and stem. So, our case is not that of cultivation of cannabis but falls in the definition of possession of ready product known as ganja.”

Also Read | Beyond Holi and bhang, the many uses of cannabis – from medicine to rope-making

Inspector AC Damor of Vinchhiya police station similarly said that Panchala had been booked for cultivation because the police found standing cannabis plants in his field, rather than a harvested product.

When is cannabis cultivation legal?

The NDPS Act generally prohibits the unauthorised cultivation of cannabis plants as well as the production, manufacture, possession, sale, purchase, transport and consumption of narcotic drugs. However, there are exceptions for cannabis, with state-level rules allowing licensed cultivation for scientific or medicinal purposes.

Story continues below this ad

Uttarakhand and Madhya Pradesh have legalised cannabis cultivation for several years. Himachal Pradesh joined them in July, permitting the controlled cultivation of cannabis for medicinal and scientific purposes.

‘We got this before GTA 6’: Why the BJP and Congress are invoking a viral meme in their political battle
content_html:
GTA 6's launch sparked a political exchange in India, with BJP highlighting the country's progress since 2013 and Congress questioning Modi's gaming imagery. (X/Narendra Modi, Rockstar Games)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

The launch of Grand Theft Auto VI has given India’s political parties a new reference point in their social media messaging, with the BJP and Congress drawing on the video game’s popularity to trade political barbs.

The exchange centres on a popular internet joke about the 13-year gap between GTA V, released in 2013, and its successor, which launched worldwide on Thursday (November 19).

The BJP, including Prime Minister Narendra Modi, used the comparison to highlight what it describes as India’s progress over this period. The Congress has questioned the ruling party’s decision to associate itself with a game built around criminal activity and violence.

India is playing a whole new game! https://t.co/CMkMbK6vII

— Narendra Modi (@narendramodi) November 19, 2026

First, what is GTA?

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

First released in 1997, Grand Theft Auto is an open-world video game franchise in which players explore fictional American cities, undertake missions and engage in activities ranging from driving and exploration to theft and violent crime.

Developed by Rockstar Games, the series has become known for its sprawling virtual worlds, satirical portrayal of American society and the freedom it gives players to interact with their surroundings. Its best-known instalments include GTA III, Vice City, San Andreas, GTA IV and GTA V.

Players can move freely through these virtual worlds, travelling on foot or by vehicle, and undertake missions involving everything from petty theft to organised crime. The games also recreate aspects of everyday life, including phone calls and messages, while using fictional characters and businesses to satirise American society.

MUST READ | How Grand Theft Auto changed gaming, and why GTA VI has so much to live up to

GTA VI follows Jason and Lucia, a couple involved in criminal activity in a fictionalised version of Florida. Like its predecessors, the game features violence and criminal missions alongside an expansive world that players can explore.

And what is the meme?

Story continues below this ad

The political exchange draws on a meme that became popular during the long wait for GTA VI: “We got [something] before GTA VI.” Internet users inserted major political events, technological developments and other milestones into the phrase to joke about how much had changed since the previous instalment.

The 13-year gap made the joke particularly adaptable to political messaging. For the BJP, it offered a way to present its account of changes in India since 2013 using a reference familiar to younger audiences. For the Congress, the game’s criminal themes provided an opportunity to ridicule the Prime Minister’s choice of imagery.

The franchise’s popularity added to the attention surrounding the exchange. Rockstar Games, the game’s publisher, said GTA VI generated $3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day, describing it as the biggest entertainment launch in history.

How has the BJP used GTA VI?

As anticipation surrounding the game’s release grew, the Prime Minister’s X and Instagram accounts published a series of slides borrowing the franchise’s distinctive typography and imagery.

Story continues below this ad

“Between GTA V and VI, here’s how India upgraded”, the post stated, followed by images of ‘Level Up’ across various sectors from the economy and poverty alleviation to ramping up its solar power generation capacity and start-up ecosystem.

Also Read | GTA 6, Modi and the BJP’s bid to crack the Gen Z audience

The campaign used the period between the two releases to showcase the government’s claims about India’s economic growth, infrastructure development and other achievements.

According to BJP sources, the party’s social media workers had identified the trend before the game’s launch. However, the decision to capitalise on it was made following Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi’s recent interaction with students at US universities.

On Saturday (November 21), Minister of Road Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari’s social media account used similar imagery to highlight highway construction and reductions in travel time across the country.

Story continues below this ad

Several BJP state units and accounts associated with senior leaders, including Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma, also amplified the trend.

Why has the Congress objected?

The Congress attacked the Prime Minister’s choice of imagery, pointing to the game’s central themes of crime and violence.

Congress communications in-charge Jairam Ramesh criticised the Prime Minister’s post, referring to GTA VI’s protagonists, Jason and Lucia, who are involved in criminal activity. He said in a post, “The PM in a desperate bid to reach out to the youth has resorted to GTA V and GTA VI imagery on social media. Recall that this video game follows a criminal duo. How very appropriate.”

The BJP responded by accusing the Congress of focusing on the video game’s storyline rather than engaging with the figures presented in Modi’s post.

Story continues below this ad

BJP social media co-convenor Priti Gandhi said the post was “about exposing Congress-era failures & showcasing India’s progress” since 2014. “You were unable to counter a single figure, so you chose to moralise about video-game characters…” she alleged.

The Congress also circulated a minute-long video highlighting the game’s violent themes, captioned “From Vote Chori To GTA: Modi’s Perfect Match”.
